title: Local Government Pension Scheme (CAS-52188-D3K5)
text:
CAS-52188-D3K5
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr W
Scheme Local Government Pension Scheme (the Scheme)
Respondent Plymouth Community Homes (the Employer)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
As relevant, extracts from the Local Government Pensions Scheme Regulations 2013
(the Regulations) are set out in the Appendix. Briefly, the Regulations provide for
three tiers of IHER benefits depending upon the member’s incapacity for future
employment. In order to qualify for any IHER benefits, the member must be deemed:
• permanently incapable1 of discharging the duties of their current employment; and
• not immediately capable of undertaking any gainful employment2.
If the member satisfies these conditions, the tier of benefits awarded depends upon
their level of future incapacity for work, as follows:-
Tier 1 The member is considered unlikely to be capable of undertaking
gainful employment before normal pension age (NPA).
1 Defined by the Regulations to mean “that the member will more likely than not, be incapable until, at the
earliest, his/her [normal pension age]. Mr W’s normal pension age is 67.
2 Defined by the Regulations as paid employment for at least 30 hours each week for at least 12 months.
1
John Bristow
Plymouth Community Homes

CAS-52188-D3K5
Tier 2 The member is considered unlikely to be capable of undertaking any
gainful employment within three years of leaving employment, but is
likely to be capable of such before NPA.
Tier 3 The member is considered likely to be capable of undertaking gainful
employment within three years of leaving employment (or before NPA
if this is sooner).
The Regulations are supported by the Statutory Ill Health Retirement Guidance -
September 2014 (the Guidance)3. The Guidance was issued under Regulation 36(4)
of the Regulations. Scheme employers and Independent Registered Medical
Practitioners (IRMP) must take the Guidance into consideration when undertaking
their functions under Regulations 36 to 38 of the Regulations (see appendix).
The Scheme employer must understand the reasoning behind the opinion and IHER
certificate issued by the IRMP under Regulations 36. So, paragraph 20 of the
Guidance recommends that the IRMP provides a narrative report as well as the
certificate. Paragraph 23 of the Guidance provides that:
“In addressing questions about permanent incapacity, whether in terms of the
local government employment or gainful employment elsewhere,
consideration must, therefore, be given not to the immediate or foreseeable
future, but to the date when the member attains their normal pension age.
…
Consideration should include whether that treatment is readily available and
appropriate for the member and whether, with treatment, the member is likely
to become capable before normal pension age. The fact that the member
might choose not to accept such treatment should not be a relevant factor.
Treatment can include lifestyle changes such as weight loss and stopping the
use of harmful substances such as tobacco and alcohol. It would not be
appropriate to consider the release of ill health retirement benefits for a reason
other than when the member was genuinely medically incapacitated from
undertaking their current employment or any other employment at the point of
departure.”
In early 2017, Mr W applied for IHER following a breakdown in his health related to
various conditions and their symptoms.
On 10 October 2017, Dr P Yarnley, an occupational health physician for IMASS, was
appointed as the IRMP responsible for reviewing Mr W’s IHER application. Dr Yarnley
took note of Mr W’s occupation as a full-time multi-skilled electrician for the Employer,
and that he was 60 at the time of his application. He understood that he was required
to consider if Mr W was permanently incapable of discharging efficiently the duties of
his role due to ill health or infirmity of body or mind. In drafting his opinion, Dr Yarnley
3 https://lgpslibrary.org/assets/statgui/ew/20140917IHG.pdf
2

CAS-52188-D3K5
took note of the following medical evidence, medical conditions, and undertaken
treatments:
Medical evidence
• occupational health file;
• GP report of 30 June 2017;
• job description;
• consultant orthopaedic report of 14 August 2017; and
• Derriford audiology report of 22 April 2016.
Medical conditions
• osteoarthritis;
• bilateral total knee replacement;
• reduced hearing;
• myocardial infraction (2014);
• stress; and
• hand vibration associated problems.
Treatment
• bilateral knee replacements;
• stents to the arteries supplying blood to the heart (2014);
• aspirin – to reduce risk of further myocardial infraction;
• metoprolol – to help reduce risk of future heart problems;
• ramipril - to help reduce risk of future heart problems;
• atoravastin – to reduce cholesterol;
• paracetamol, codeine, amitriptyline and oramorph for pain management.
A summary of Dr Yarnley’s report (the 2017 Report) is set out below in paragraphs
10 and 19.
Mr W underwent bilateral knee replacements in 2013 and in 2016. The consultant
orthopaedic report of August 2017 said that Mr W had a good range of movement in
both knees before he was discharged from physiotherapy. In spite of this, Mr W could
only walk for 45 minutes, he was unable to stand in any one position, squat or kneel,
and his lifting capability was reduced. Mr W reported severe pain in both knees and
that he had previously fallen due to instability. It was noted that he was not
undertaking as much exercise as recommended by his treating physicians. It was
possible that his knee instability was due to reduced muscle strength secondary to a
lack of use.
Mr W’s current level of pain and functional level of impairment was not consistent with
the comments made by the orthopaedic department on his discharge. Further
investigations were required to establish why his positive recovery halted, and to
3

CAS-52188-D3K5
formulate a new treatment plan. This would help establish if his current pain relief
medication was appropriate, or if more effective medication could be prescribed.
In terms of future treatments, Dr Yardley suggested a surgical review to see if further
intervention was required; additional physiotherapy; and a review of his pain
medication. These treatments would help to improve Mr W’s functional capacity in
regard to his knee pain, though, it was unlikely that he could return to his role. It was,
however, likely that he could undertake gainful employment such as office
administrative work, customer service or reception work.
The Derriford audiology report from 2016 noted that Mr W claimed his hearing loss
was around 80% in each ear. However, a hearing loss test conducted by IMASS
indicated that there was no substantial change in his hearing since 2008. While Mr W
did report difficulty in communicating with others on the job when there was moderate
background noise, digital hearing aids would be expected to help overcome any
disablement. Mr W had been able to function in his workplace, and the alternative
roles suggested would not be associated with high background noise. His hearing
loss would not result in a material disadvantage to employment.
There was no evidence of Mr W’s heart and vibration white finger4 condition
impacting his ability to undertake his role or any other alternative gainful employment.
A functional assessment from April 2017 said that he was able to use a keyboard
without any functional impairment. The medication he took for his heart condition
helped to prevent any future cardiac events, but it would not restrict his employment
abilities.
He (Dr Yarnley) was asked to consider, on the balance of probabilities, if Mr W was
expected to undertake other gainful employment. His opinion was that while Mr W
was prevented from undertaking his own role with the Employer, Mr W was not
immediately permanently prevented from undertaking alternative gainful employment.
The evidence did not suggest that his conditions would reduce the likelihood that he
could also obtain alternative employment. Allowing for regular breaks and reasonable
adjustments.
In order to satisfy the first condition of the IHER criteria, it needed to be accepted that
all appropriate treatments for the illness/condition had been undertaken. In his view,
Mr W was prevented from returning to his role due to the ongoing symptoms
associated with his knee condition. This was likely to be permanent until his NPA.
In considering the second condition for IHER, gainful employment, Dr Yarnley took
into account the following conditions/treatments:-
4 A condition caused by prolonged exposure to vibrating tools. Symptoms of the condition are numbness,
tingling and whitening of the fingertips during exposure to the cold or vibrations. Treatments for the condition
include a reduction in the use of vibration tools.
4

CAS-52188-D3K5
• Persistent knee pain affecting Mr W’s ability to walk, sit, stand, lift and carry. While
he was not receiving any treatments, on balance, with pain management and
future physiotherapy, he could undertake gainful employment.
• Reduced hearing had not affected his role with the Employer, nor was it expected
to hinder his ability to undertake gainful employment. The use of digital hearing
aids would improve his functional capacity.
• Cardiac and vibration conditions would not prevent Mr W from engaging in any
gainful employment. Mr W was receiving appropriate medication for his cardiac
condition.
• Stress – It was accepted that Mr W had previously had difficulty in adjusting to
changes in his work environment. However, Dr Yarnley considered this to be a
behavioural issue, not a medical one.
Based on the evidence available, Mr W was permanently prevented from undertaking
the duties of his role up to his NPA. However, while he was currently prevented from
undertaking gainful employment, it was expected that Mr W would be able to
undertake gainful employment of a sedentary nature within three years of leaving
employment. Dr Yarnley completed an IHER certificate and provided a copy to the
Employer in support of his view.
The 2017 Report said that if Mr W wished to appeal the matter, the Employer was to
follow its own Internal Dispute Resolution Procedure (IDRP) before submitting any
appeals to IMASS about the IRMP’s opinion.
On 10 November 2017, Mr W attended a capability hearing with the Employer, his
trade union representative, the electrical contracts manager and a HR business
partner. During the meeting it was noted that:-
• The Employer had offered to support him in finding a new role within the
organisation, which he declined.
• The 2017 Report made clear that he was permanently incapable or undertaking
his role. It was agreed that his employment would be terminated on capability
grounds effective from 17 November 2017. He was entitled to 12 weeks’ pay in
lieu of notice and the payment of any untaken holiday entitlement.
• Based on Dr Yarnley’s opinion he was eligible for a Tier 3 IHER pension. The
reasoning for this was outlined in the 2017 Report.
On 16 November 2017, the Employer wrote to Mr W to confirm that his employment
was terminated effective from 17 November 2017. He was entitled to a Tier 3 IHER
award, the reasoning for which had been discussed with him and his representative,
at length, prior to the capability meeting. Further details about his IHER entitlement
would shortly be sent to him, including information on his appeal rights, if he wished
to dispute the decision/Tier award.
5

CAS-52188-D3K5
On 25 April 2019, Peninsula Pensions, the Scheme administrator, wrote to the
Employer and said that it had been 18 months since Mr W began receiving his Tier 3
pension. In accordance with the Regulations, it needed to review his IHER
entitlement. It asked the Employer to refer Mr W to the Scheme IRMP for an
assessment, thereafter a copy of the IRMP’s report needed to be forwarded to
Peninsula Pensions.
On 10 June 2019, Dr Aly, an IRMP for Medigold, the Employer’s new occupational
health adviser, wrote to Mr W’s GP to request an up-to-date overview of his health.
On 30 July 2019, Dr Leman, Mr W’s GP, responded to Dr Aly and said:
“at present [Mr W] is suffering from some chest pain. He has on-going bilateral
knee pain and on-going stress and anger management issues. He also
experiences tinnitus and hearing loss and symptoms from his vibration white
finger.
…
Most of [Mr W’s] conditions are chronic and longstanding and are therefore
unlikely to improve”
On 18 September 2019, Mr W attended a face-to-face appointment with Dr Parker,
the IRMP responsible for conducting the 18-month review.
On 10 October 2019, Dr Parker provided a copy of his opinion to Mr W and the
Employer which said that:-
• On reviewing an up-to-date GP report for Mr W, it was clear that the sum total of
his conditions symptoms was having a greater impact than they would individually
suggest. His continued knee pain limited his range of movement to nothing more
than walking a few hundred meters. He was unable to sit or stand in one position
without changing position regularly.
• He experienced shortness of breath, possibly due to a previous myocardial
infraction. He struggled to hear voices even with low level background noise.
• Mr W was unlikely to be capable of undertaking gainful employment within three
years of his leaving date; however, it was likely he would be able to before his
NPA.
On 22 October 2019, the Employer asked Peninsula Pensions if it required any
additional paperwork. Section B2 of the IHER review certificate was signed by Dr
Parker “unlikely to be capable of gainful employment within three years of the leaving
shown in part A” (17 November 2017). They asked for clarity on whether Mr W was
now due any further reviews.
On 24 January 2020, Peninsula Pensions responded to the Employer and explained
that it needed to determine if Mr W was eligible for protections under the 1997 section
6

CAS-52188-D3K5
of the Regulations. Section B11 of the 2017 IHER certificate was completed by Dr
Yarnley, which said “is not – on the balance of probabilities, is permanently incapable
of discharging efficiently the duties of his/her employment or any other comparable
employment with his/her employer because of ill health or infirmity of mind or body”.
This was in response to Dr Yarnley being asked if Mr W met the criteria for IHER
under old IHER test under the 1997 Section of the Scheme, in 2017. It asked for
confirmation if this still applied in regard to increasing Mr W’s Tier 3 pension to a Tier
2 award.
On 17 February 2020, the Employer responded to Peninsula Pensions and said that
Mr W satisfied the “old test” under the 1997 section of the Regulations, based on the
18-month review findings. It forwarded a copy of the IHER certificate signed by Dr
Parker in support of this.
In February 2020, Mr W submitted an appeal under stage one of the Scheme’s IDRP
and said that:-
• The 2017 Report was actually based on a previous capability report by a Dr
Parker from when he had his first knee replacement, three years prior. He also did
not attend a face-to-face assessment with Dr Yarnley.
• He originally appealed the decision to award him a Tier 3 pension on three
occasions with the help of the Employer’s Head of HR. This was directly against
IMASS in relation to Dr Yarnley’s medical advice. They believed that he ought to
have been entitled to a Tier 1 award in 2017. They highlighted that not all of his
conditions were taken into account. On review, Dr Yarnley did not agree to
change his opinion or amend the 2017 Report.
• During his Tier 3 review assessment, he shared some personal information about
his feelings towards the assessment in 2017, and his anger towards not having a
face-to-face assessment with Dr Yarnley. Thereafter, the report he received was
for another patient with their personal information outlined. He raised this serious
data breach with Medigold directly.
• He attended a face-to-face assessment with Dr Parker, the IRMP who conducted
his original assessment before Dr Yarnley took over in 2017. He asked Dr Parker
if an individual with one knee replacement was more capable that an individual
with two knee replacements. He also provided a copy of the capability report Dr
Yarnley based the 2017 Report on.
• He pointed to Dr Parker’s signature on the capability report and asked if it was his
signature. To which Dr Parker replied that it looked like it had been electronically
signed. Dr Parker said it was unlikely that he would sign an out-of-date report. So,
he (Mr W) believed that the capability report was signed by someone else.
• After Dr Parker reviewed the applicable medical evidence, in addition to an up-to-
date GP report, the decision was made to increase his award to Tier 2. This
meant that he was incapable of gainful employment within three years of leaving
7

CAS-52188-D3K5
his role, but he would be capable before his NPA. He was almost 66, and he had
not worked for five years. So, the likelihood of him finding employment before his
NPA was unlikely.
• Since the 18-month review he was diagnosed with a serious condition in his right
ankle, for which he had an orthopaedic appointment in February 2020.
• He suffered substantial distress during the IHER assessments and reviews and
hoped that the additional evidence provided was enough to increase his award to
Tier 1.
On 24 February 2020, Peninsula Pensions telephoned Mr W to clarify whether his
complaint was about the decision to award him a Tier 3 pension or if it was about the
recent 18-month review which resulted in his Tier 3 award being increased to a Tier 2
award. In response, Mr W explained that he was complaining about the process
undertaken in reviewing his entitlement in 2017. During this call, Peninsula Pensions
explained that as he was complaining about a decision that occurred more than six
months ago, there was no requirement for the Employer to accept his complaint.
On 4 March 2020, Peninsula Pensions told Mr W that it had forwarded his complaint
onto the Employer to consider under stage one of the IDRP. A full response was due
to be sent to him by 24 April 2020. It explained that a Tier 3 benefit could only be
increased to Tier 2, not Tier 1. It understood that his complaint was that his IHER
application was mishandled, and that he ought to have been entitled to a Tier 1
award. The Employer was only required to consider complaints within six months of
the original decision being complained about. If the Employer agreed to consider his
complaint under stage one IDRP, and he did not agree with the response, he could
then ask for it to be considered under stage two of the IDRP. Peninsula Pensions was
responsible for providing stage two IDRP responses.
On 12 March 2020, the Employer’s Head of HR responded to Peninsula Pensions
and said that he spent a substantial amount of time with Mr W, in 2017, advising him
of the IHER and appeals process. So, he did not agree that Mr W was unaware of his
right to appeal the decision to award him a Tier 3 pension at the time. Consequently,
the Employer did not agree to accept his complaint due to the amount of time that
had passed, and Mr W’s awareness of his appeal rights.
On 30 March 2020, Peninsula Pensions provided Mr W with confirmation that his
annual pension had increased from £8,427.12 to £10,899.10, effective from 18
September 2019. It had also raised an arrears payment equal to the difference
between his Tier 3 and Tier 2 entitlement between 18 September 2019 and 30 March
2020.
On 26 May 2020, Mr W telephoned Peninsula Pensions for an update on his IDRP
appeal/complaint. During this telephone call, Mr W was advised that the Employer did
not agree to accept his IDRP complaint as it was out of time.
8

CAS-52188-D3K5
On 29 May 2020, Peninsula Pensions wrote to Mr W and said it understood that the
basis of his complaint related to old/incorrect reports being relied on by the Employer
when he was awarded a Tier 3 pension. The fact his award was increased recently to
Tier 2, in his view supported the fact an error was made in 2017. It said, the Employer
had chosen not to accept his IDRP complaint, as it was received six months after the
Tier 3 decision was made. Consequently, it was unable to review or accept a stage
two IDRP complaint. It understood that the Employer had not contacted Mr W directly
about its decision, so it provided a copy of the Employers letter from March 2020.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
A member’s entitlements to benefits when taking early retirement due to ill-health are
determined by the scheme rules or regulations. The scheme rules or regulations
determine the circumstances in which members are eligible for ill-health benefits, the
conditions they must satisfy and the way in which decisions about ill-health benefits
must be taken.
• to continue payment of Tier 3 benefits for any period up to the maximum permitted
by regulation 35(7);
• to award Tier 2 benefits to the member from the date of the review decision if the
authority is satisfied that the member:
o is permanently incapable of discharging efficiently the duties of the
employment the member was engaged in, and
o either is unlikely to be capable of gainful employment before NPA, or is
unlikely to be capable of any gainful employment within three years of leaving
the employment, but is likely to be capable of gainful employment before
reaching NPA; or
9

CAS-52188-D3K5
• to cease payment of benefits to the member.
It was understood that Mr W’s main point of contention related to the Employer’s
decision to grant him a Tier 3 award in November 2017, based on the contents of the
2017 Report. In considering Mr W’s IHER application, Dr Yarnley took into account
the medical evidence, medication and treatments. Dr Yarnley agreed that Mr W met
the two IHER conditions under regulation 35. So, Mr W was deemed permanently
incapable of undertaking the duties of his role and not immediately capable of gainful
employment.
The 2017 Report explained that while Mr W’s knee pain prevented him from
undertaking his role, and immediate gainful employment, he would likely benefit from
further surgical consultation, physiotherapy and a review of his pain medication.
Further, Dr Yarnley did not agree that Mr W’s other conditions (hearing loss, cardiac
issues, vibration, or stress) would impact his ability to undertake gainful employment.
On the balance of probabilities, it was unlikely that Mr W’s conditions would prevent
him from undertaking gainful employment within three years of leaving employment,
or before his NPA if sooner.
Mr W has made reference to a capability report, from 2013, but dated from April
2017, that Dr Yarnley relied upon when drafting the 2017 Report. He has inferred that
the decision to award him a Tier 3 pension, should not have been based on this
report due to it being, in his view, out of date.
It was for Dr Yarnley to decide how much weight to apply to any piece of medical
evidence he was presented. While the capability report is referred to in the 2017
Report, it was the Adjudicator’s view that sufficient alternative medical evidence was
available to Dr Yarnley when he drafted the 2017 Report. Given the documents listed
by Dr Yarnley in the 2017 Report, it was clear that all available evidence was
considered. Overall, it was accepted that Dr Yarnley understood and acted in
accordance with the relevant Regulations and the Guidance.
Mr W commented on the likelihood of him being able to undertake gainful
employment at his age (60 and seven years away from his NPA). However,
paragraph 27 of the Guidance stated:
“Non-medical factors, such as the general availability of gainful employment in
a particular area or the attitude to certain conditions, would not be material
factors and should not be part of the independent registered medical
practitioner’s consideration, while the effect a medical condition would have on
their practical ability to undertake gainful employment would.”
So, there was no requirement for the IRMP, or the decision maker, to comment on
the availability of any suggested form of gainful employment. In accordance with the
Guidance, Dr Yarnley suggested that Mr W might be able to work in customer
services (reception), office administrative work, or anything of a sedentary nature.
10

CAS-52188-D3K5
On receipt of the 2017 Report, the Employer made the decision to award Mr W a Tier
3 pension. There were no errors or omissions of fact for the Employer to consider
when reviewing the 2017 Report. The findings outlined in the 2017 Report were made
in accordance with the Guidance and the Regulations. Dr Yarnley was clear in his
view that Mr W was permanently unable to undertake his role, but that his incapacity
and resultant symptoms were unlikely to prevent him from attaining gainful
employment within three years of leaving.
The Adjudicator’s opinion was that there was no apparent reason why the Employer
should not have accepted the findings of the 2017 Report. It was based on sufficient
relevant information, and so, the outcome reached by the Employer was supported by
the evidence. There is no material reason why the Employer should be required to re-
consider its decision to award Mr W a Tier 3 pension in 2017.
As the Employer and Peninsula Pensions had explained, Mr W’s Tier 3 pension could
only be increased from Tier 3 to Tier 2, on review. This was in accordance with the
provision set out under Regulation 37(7)(b).
Mr W referred to a delay in increasing his Tier 3 pension to Tier 2. Based on the
submissions provided by Peninsula Pensions this was partially due to the need for
the Employer to confirm if Mr W was eligible for protections under the 1997 section of
the Regulations. Once it was established that Mr W was entitled to these protections,
his pension was increased to Tier 2 on 30 March 2020, with any arrears from 18
September 2019 to 30 March 2020 paid to Mr W. Overall, while there was a slight
delay in increasing the Tier level of Mr W’s entitlement, the delay was not
unreasonable.
The Adjudicator was satisfied that a proper decision-making process was undertaken
by the Employer (in 2017). So, there were no grounds to remit the matter back to the
Employer.
Mr W did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion, and the complaint was passed to me
to consider. Mr W provided his further comments which do not change the outcome. I
agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion and note the additional points raised by Mr W,
which are:-
• The functional capability assessment undertaken by Dr Parker, in 2013, was
invalid. He submitted that despite being signed by Dr Parker on 27 April 2017, the
report was based off a telephone consultation he underwent in 2013.
• During the 18-month Tier 3 review, he asked Dr Parker if they signed the
functional capability report, to which Dr Parker said they had not. Dr Parker said
that his capability had significantly reduced; however, he was only eligible for a
Tier 2 award as his Tier 3 award could not be increased to Tier 1. He believed that
this demonstrated that the initial Tier 3 award was incorrect.
• His former Head of HR agreed to support him through the IHER process and
believed that he would likely meet the criteria for a Tier 1 award. The Head of HR
11

CAS-52188-D3K5
was shocked when he was only awarded Tier 3 and said that he would support Mr
W in appealing the matter.
Ombudsman’s decision
Briefly, Regulation 35 provides entitlement to an IHER award if both conditions under
regulations 35(3) and (4) are met. That is:
• as a result of ill-health or infirmity of mind or body, the applicant is permanently
incapable of discharging efficiently the duties of the employment they were
engaged in; and
12

CAS-52188-D3K5
• they are, as a result of ill-health or infirmity of mind or body,
not immediately capable of undertaking any gainful employment.
As and when these conditions are met, the IRMP needs to consider the extent of the
applicants’ incapacity. This is done by making a decision on what Tier of benefits the
applicant is entitled to. See paragraph 4 above for the explanations of each Tier and
the necessary criteria that needs to be met for an award.
Regulation 36 provides that before any decisions can be made, the scheme
employer/administering authority must consider an IHER application in consultation
with the Scheme appointed IRMP. In line with the provisions of Regulation 36, the
IRMP needs to test the applicant's eligibility for IHER against regulation 35 and
provide an IHER certificate. The Guidance provides that the IRMP should provide
a narrative report, alongside the certificate, to help the decision maker understand
their view.
The decision as to whether Mr W met the IHER criteria was for the Employer to make
as the decision maker in consultation with the Scheme appointed IRMP. Overall, I am
satisfied that the application and interpretation of the relevant rules/regulations, in
considering Mr W’s Tier entitlement, was undertaken by the correct party, that is the
Employer. So, there is nothing further to consider on this point as there is no basis for
which this can be challenged, nor would it be successful if it was.
The medical evidence obtained and considered
The Employer placed most of its weight on the 2017 Report by Dr Yarnley, which said
that:-
• Mr W underwent bilateral total knee replacements in 2013 and in 2016. After the
second replacement his consultant surgeon said he had a good range of
movement in both knees with physiotherapy achieving a positive outcome post
surgery.
• He said he was unable to sit, stand or walk for more than 45 minutes, nor was he
able to squat or kneel, and he had a reduced lifting capability. This was at odds
with the comments of his consultant surgeon, though he had not yet been referred
to the consultant despite the severe knee pain he still experienced. Further
investigations into his pain were required.
• The following treatments were recommended: a surgical review for his knees to
see if further intervention was needed; physiotherapy to help reduce pain and
improve knee stability; and a review of his pain medication.
Overall, based on the evidence provided, the IRMP’s opinion was that:-
• Mr W was “unable to return to his own role due to his knee condition and the
persistence of symptoms and significant functional restrictions despite a bilateral
knee replacement”. However, he had not yet undertaken any treatment for his
knee pain.
13

CAS-52188-D3K5
• On the balance of probabilities, “it was expected that with improved pain
management and potentially further physiotherapy he would be able to undertake
gainful employment, but not immediately”.
• His hearing loss, heart condition and vibration white finger were unlikely to act as
a barrier in undertaking gainful employment. Stress was not a condition but a
symptom of one and was not a relevant factor in assessing his incapacity.
• In term of Mr W’s ability to undertake gainful employment:
“[Mr W’s] health problems would not prevent him from undertaking gainful
employment and [I] do not consider his medical conditions should reduce the
likelihood for a properly motivated person of obtaining such employment when
allowing for reasonable adjustments and health and safety guidance relating to
the need to take regular micro breaks when working in a sedentary role”.
• Overall:
“based on the evidence available at the time of the assessment, [Mr W’s] ill-heath
or infirmity of mind or body render them, on the balance of probabilities, before
their retirement age permanently incapable of discharging efficiently the duties of
their current employment, expected to be able to obtain gainful employment
before normal retirement age; but would be expected to be able to obtain gainful
employment within three years.”
Based on the evidence presented and available to the IRMP, I am satisfied that the
Dr Yarnley assessed all the available evidence and decided the weight to apply to
each individual piece of information.
I understand that there is some contention from Mr W about the validity of a functional
capability report dated April 2017, which he argues was completed in 2013. As I have
said, it was for the IRMP to weigh each piece of evidence accordingly. I find that in
addition to the capability report, the IRMP was in receipt of sufficient information to
allow them to form a view on Mr W’s eligibility for IHER. Based on the contents of the
2017 Report, the IRMP appears to have applied the most weight to the Consultant
Orthopaedic Surgeons report of 14 August 2017.
Overall, I am satisfied that the IRMP’s 2017 Report covered the appropriate test for
IHER in line with the applicable 2013 Regulations and Guidance. The IRMP made
clear that their view was, on balance, that Mr W was not immediately capable of
gainful employment, but that he would likely be within the next three years. The 2017
Report provided an overview of likely prognosis and treatment pathways for Mr W’s
incapacity to allow for a return to gainful employment of a sedentary nature, with
reasonable adjustments, before his NPA of 67, some seven years away. There was
no obvious error, omission of fact, or misunderstanding of the relevant regulations to
consider.
14

CAS-52188-D3K5
Broadly, the Employer accepted the view of the IMRP that Mr W, in 2017, met the
criteria for a Tier 3 award. I understand that Mr W has argued that the Employer was
initially supportive of his IHER application with an expectation that he would be
eligible for Tier 1; however, on receipt of the 2017 Report, the Employer made the
decision to only award him Tier 3 benefits.
As I have previously highlighted, the Employer can only be expected to review Mr W’s
IHER application from a lay perspective. It is not for the Employer to query the
medical opinion provided by the IRMP. However, the Employer is expected to take
account of any errors, omissions of fact, or misunderstanding of the 2013
Regulations. I am satisfied that the Employer has fulfilled its function as the decision
maker as there are no errors of note within the 2017 Report.
Overall, I find that the Employer’s decision was supported by the available evidence,
and it:
• applied the law and scheme rules/regulations correctly;
• asked itself the right questions; and
• only took into account relevant factors.
I appreciate that following the mandatory 18-month review of Mr W’s Tier 3 award a
decision was made to uplift his award to Tier 2, which he believes is a sign of a flaw
in the original decision making in 2017.
However, the decision to uplift Mr W’s benefits to Tier 2 does not mean that the initial
decision to award him Tier 3 was incorrect. It just means that the expected course of
his condition/symptoms based on the available treatments was not borne out. The
views provided by the IRMPs are made on the balance of probability. So, there will
always be an element of uncertainty about prognosis. An assessment as to the
propriety of the decision-making process should not apply the benefit of hindsight.
While I appreciate that this will not be the outcome that Mr W had hoped for, there is
no maladministration or errors of any merit to consider. Consequently, there are no
grounds to remit the decision back to the Employer to reconsider.
I do not uphold Mr W’s complaint.
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman/Deputy Pension Ombudsman
11 July 2026
15

title: Vanguard Self Invested Personal Pension (CAS-119011-R3F8)
text:
CAS-119011-R3F8
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr N
Scheme Vanguard Self Invested Personal Pension (the SIPP)
Respondents Vanguard Asset Management Limited (Vanguard)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
On 29 June 2023, an employer contribution of £180,000 was made into Mr N’s SIPP.
It was intended that this contribution would not result in Mr N exceeding his annual
allowance, on the basis of annual allowance carried forward1 from previous tax years.
On 24 August 2023, Mr N submitted his year-end accounts to his accountant
(Personal Investor Services).
On 5 September 2023, Personal Investor Services informed Mr N that only a £60,000
contribution should have been paid to comply with the carry forward requirements. A
payment in excess of this amount would result in an additional tax charge. In order to
benefit from the carry forward provisions Mr N would have needed to:-
• Have had relevant UK earnings in the current tax year exceeding the amount of
the contribution;
• Have used his full available allowance in the current tax year and have available
unused annual allowance in the previous years;
1 This allows a member to use unused annual allowance from the last three tax years to potential allow to save more into their pension
in a given tax year.
1

CAS-119011-R3F8
• Have had a UK registered pension scheme in their name for the years in question,
including as either an active or deferred member.
On the same day, Mr N contacted Vanguard about the issue, and it recommended
that he speak to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and Pensionwise. Mr
N contacted HMRC twice and Pensionwise, and says he was told that according to
the Pensions Tax Manual (PTM) a genuine contribution error2 refund can be made at
a scheme administrators’ discretion.
On 22 September 2023, Mr N contacted Vanguard to put forward a case of genuine
error. Mr N was told about refunded excess contributions following the tax year end
and the process of refunding excess contributions was described. This process
included providing the following documents: a copy of his P60, a copy of his self-
assessment tax return and a letter from his accountant confirming his earnings for the
tax year.
On 30 September 2023, Mr N replied to Vanguard maintaining that he could not
provide the requested documents until 2024 and as such he did not think it was being
treated as a genuine error by Vanguard.
On 5 October 2023, Vanguard replied to Mr N reaffirming that no refund could be
made and that the excess payment could only be returned by suppling the
documents requested previously.
On 22 October 2023, Mr N asked for a second opinion and to escalate his request
under the genuine error rules.
On 18 September 2024, Vanguard provided its response to Mr N’s complaint which
can be summarised as follows:-
• HMRC guidelines do not allow a refund of excess employer contributions.
• HMRC guidelines do not extend to miscalculations. Vanguard has not made any
errors, and its procedures have been followed correctly.
• As a result, Mr N’s complaint cannot be upheld.
• Due to the amount of time that it has taken to resolve this complaint Vanguard
offered £50 once Mr N updated his bank details on his Vanguard account.
On 20 September 2024, Mr N responded to the outcome of Vanguard’s formal
decision and raised the following points:-
• He had verbally informed his accountant of his contribution but did not take
specific advice.
2
PTM146100 - Other authorised payments: genuine errors: overview and principle of promptly rectified payments errors
2

CAS-119011-R3F8
• He had misunderstood the carry forward rules and believed that he had been
using up the 3rd year’s allowance before it was lost and he was not aware of the
rule that stated that the initial contribution was treated as the first year’s
allowance.
• He had made a genuine error and not a miscalculation.
• He disagreed that “HMRC guidelines do not allow a refund of excess of employer
contributions” and believed that HMRC does not refer to employer contributions
made in error.
• HMRC provides guidance on the refund of personal pension contributions made in
error if a refund is requested within four weeks. In this case the excess contribute
can be refunded. As Mr N notified Vanguard within a reasonable period, he should
have the contribution refunded.
• He contacted Vanguard immediately after he was notified of the overpayment.
• Without the refund he will incur an additional tax liability.
• He requested that either the contributions are refunded, or Vanguard pays for the
additional tax liability of £12,000 to put him back in the correct position.
On 1 October 2024, Vanguard responded to Mr N and explained that it was unable to
uphold his complaint and that it would await the outcome from The Pensions
Ombudsman (TPO).
On 26 March 2026, Vanguard provided TPO with copies of its Key Features
Document (KFD) and Terms and Conditions for Mr N’s SIPP as they were on 29 June
2023. These documents included the following points:-
‘What happens if I exceed the Annual Allowance or Money Purchase Annual
Allowance?
‘If the total pension contributions paid across all your pension schemes for the
tax year (including any amount carried forward from previous years), exceed
your available Annual Allowance, then you will be liable for a tax charge on the
excess. The charge is based on your marginal income tax rate (i.e. the highest
rate at which you pay tax on your income).’ (KFD - Appendix Three)
‘19 Contributions to your Vanguard Pension Plan
You will retain responsibility at all times for ensuring that any Contributions you
make, or which are paid on your behalf, to your Pension Account are within
any allowances as applicable to you. If Contributions made by you, or on your
behalf, exceed any applicable allowances in any given tax year, you will be
liable for the return of any outstanding tax liabilities to HMRC.’ (Terms and
Conditions - Appendix Four)
3

CAS-119011-R3F8
Summary of Mr N’s position
The overpayment of contributions was a genuine mistake based on what he believed
was financial advice from his accountant, and he notified Vanguard as soon as he
was aware of the mistake. On this basis Vanguard is able to return the overpaid
contributions to him and should have done so to avoid an unnecessary tax charge.
Summary of Vanguard’s position
The cancellation rights for contributions into a pension would only apply to personal
contributions or third-party contributions. As Mr N contributed an employer
contribution into his pension this criteria would not apply. Based on HMRC guidance,
Vanguard is not obligated to return the contributions in this case as it was not a result
of Vanguard’s maladministration.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
Overcontribution
Mr N said that he was provided with advice relating to the employer contribution of
£180,000. There is no evidence of Mr N receiving written advice to proceed with the
£180,000 contribution and Mr N has confirmed that this advice would only have been
provided verbally.
Vanguard explained that according to the Pension Tax Manuals, ‘genuine error’ does
not extend to miscalculations which would be the case whether Mr N had received
inaccurate advice or not. Although Mr N did not intend to overcontribute to his
pension the responsibility for checking the amount he was able to contribute was his.
Vanguard’s position is supported by the KFD and Terms and Conditions which Mr N
agreed to when registering his SIPP account. Both of these documents make it clear
that Mr N is responsible for any contributions he makes as well as any subsequent
tax charges. These documents do not reference to any requirement for Vanguard to
return contributions made in genuine error.
Based on Sections 188(2) and 190 and paragraph 6 Schedule 29 Finance Act 2004
(Appendix Five), the refund of excess contributions would only have been applied in
the event of the account being a personal pension rather than an employee pension
account. As Mr N’s account was an employee pension the potential refund of excess
contributions would not apply.
4

CAS-119011-R3F8
HMRC rules
Based on HMRC rules, PTM146100 and PTM146600 (Appendix One & Two) it is not
possible for Mr N to contribute more than £60,000 in one tax year as he would have
to have had relevant UK earnings in the current tax year, have used his allowance for
the current tax year and have the available remaining annual allowance in the
previous two tax years. These circumstances did not apply to Mr N as he was making
an employer contribution to his pension, and he did not have the relevant earnings in
that tax year to have used that year’s allowance. HMRC Pension Tax Manuals
PTM146100 and PTM146600 the refund of excess contributions does not extend to
miscalculations and as a result there is no requirement for Vanguard to refund the
excess contribution to Mr N. Under HMRC rules the responsibility lies with Mr N and
he is not automatically entitled to a refund of his contribution by Vanguard.
HMRC Pension Tax Manual PTM146300 (Appendix Six) relates to Other authorised
payments: genuine errors: inadvertent payments of pension instalments or lump
sums not exceeding £250. As per PTM146300 the payment would need to have been
made inadvertently and only then could it be considered as a genuine error and that
the payment made was under £250 in value. In this case the payment was made
intentionally but without an understanding of the subsequent tax liability.
Mr N realised he had made an overcontribution and took steps to notify Vanguard of
this as soon as he was aware of the issue. Mr N believes that as this was a genuine
mistake Vanguard should refund the excess contribution as he will have to pay
additional tax if the refund is not made.
Vanguard has explained that based on HMRC guidance, a potential refund did not
apply to Mr N’s circumstances as he had made an additional employer contribution,
and it was not required to refund Mr N’s over contribution as it was not a result of
Vanguard maladministration.
It had considered Mr N’s complaint fully and elected not to refund the excess
contributions.
I agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion and note the additional points raised by Mr N;
Mr N reiterated that this matter only related to whether Vanguard acted
reasonably by not refunding the overpayment when it was requested.
Mr N made the overpayment due to a misunderstanding of the carry forward
rules in that he did not appreciate the first £60,000 of any contribution is treated
as the first-year allowance.
Mr N explained that this was a genuine error, and it was noticed within a few
weeks, he did not miscalculate the payment he submitted. HMRC guidance to
members and employers provided states that where genuine errors are made
and reported reasonably quickly, the pension fund should refund the payment.
5

CAS-119011-R3F8
Ombudsman’s decision
I acknowledge that Mr N acted to resolve the issue of his overpayment as soon as he
became aware of it. It appears that Mr N made a number of attempts to explain his
mistake to Vanguard to enable it to refund his overcontribution. Mr N said that it was
a genuine error and that under HMRC rules Vanguard should have refunded the
contributions to him which would have avoided the additional tax charge he incurred.
The SIPP is governed by its Scheme Rules and Mr N participated in the SIPP on the
basis of the Terms and Conditions (subject to the Scheme Rules). Key features are
explained in the KFD. The Terms and Conditions specify that Vanguard will comply
with Applicable Regulations and Applicable Regulations are defined as including
laws, which would include the Finance Act 2004, and HMRC guidance. The Finance
Act 2004 provides that registered pension schemes such as the SIPP can make
payments to members and employers that are “authorised payments” but that any
payments that are not “authorised payments” are “unauthorised payments”. Tax
charges apply to unauthorised payments and may be payable both by the member
and the scheme administrator. The Terms and Conditions provide that Vanguard
cannot be compelled to pay an unauthorised payment (see Appendix Four).
Vanguard’s KFD and Terms and Conditions also make it clear that Mr N was
responsible for any contributions he made and any associated tax charges (see
Appendix Four).
The Terms and Conditions also make clear that, while one-off contributions paid by a
member can be cancelled within 30 days, cancellation rights do not apply to employer
contributions (see Appendix Four). As explained by Vanguard, this is consistent with
HMRC Guidance.
I note Vanguard explained the option of a refund of excess contributions but
concluded in September 2024 that HMRC guidance did not allow a refund of excess
employer contributions. I agree. Paragraph 6 of Schedule 29 to the Finance Act
2004 defines a refund of excess contributions lump sum (a type of authorised
payment) as a payment that is made in respect of a tax year in which the “excess
contributions condition is met in respect of the member. Under paragraph 6(3) the
“excess contributions condition” is met in respect of a member and a tax year if the
amount of “relievable pension contributions” (see section 188(2) and (3)) paid in
respect of the member in the tax year exceeds the maximum amount of relief to
which the member is entitled for the tax year under section 190 (annual limit for
relief). “Relievable pension contributions” under section 188(2) and (3) of the Finance
Act 2004 excludes contributions paid by an employer in respect of the member. If a
refund of the employer contribution of £180,000 does not meet the conditions for a
6

CAS-119011-R3F8
refund of excess contributions lump sum, it is an unauthorised payment as there does
not appear to be any other type of authorised payment which it would qualify as.
As such, I find that the Terms and Conditions did not provide cancellation rights in
relation to employer contributions and therefore Mr N had no cancellation rights in
relation to the employer contribution of £180,000. Further the exclusion of
cancellation rights for an employer contribution is consistent with and required by
HMRC Guidance and the limitations on refund of excess contribution lump sums in
the Finance Act 2004. These are incorporated into the terms of the SIPP as
Applicable Laws under the Terms and Conditions. The Terms and Conditions also
provide that Vanguard cannot be compelled to pay an unauthorised payment and any
refund of employer contributions paid by Mr N’s employer to Mr N would appear to be
an unauthorised payment.
I have also considered PTM146100 which provides for the repayment of contributions
in the case of “genuine errors”. I find that it addresses only inadvertent payment
errors where the payment was not intended to be made at all (or not to the extent of
the payment made); as explained in PTM 146600, the point is that the scheme is not
entitled to hold the relevant amount paid inadvertently in error. I find that the payment
by the employer of £180,000 was intentional and not an inadvertent payment, even
though it was made pursuant to a misunderstanding of the applicable tax relief. It
was made intentionally by Mr N, acting for the employer, in the belief (albeit incorrect)
that the amount would benefit from tax relief. I sympathise with Mr N as he only acted
on what he believed was genuine advice. I appreciate that Mr N made a number of
attempts to resolve this issue as soon as he was aware of it. However, based on the
Terms and Conditions of the SIPP, HMRC guidance and the Finance Act 2004, I
agree with the Adjudicator that Mr N was not entitled to a refund of his employer’s
contribution of £180,000.
Therefore, I do not uphold Mr N’s complaint.

CAS-119011-R3F8
Appendix One
PTM146100 - Other authorised payments: genuine errors: overview and principle of
promptly rectified payments errors
Genuine errors: General
As part of the day to day administration of a registered pension scheme, it is possible that
a genuine error could result in:
• an unauthorised payment seemingly being made but which is not actually a
payment at all for the purpose of the tax rules applying to the scheme, or
• an overpayment of pension being made that is an unauthorised payment
(PTM146300), or
• a contribution seemingly being made into the scheme but which is not actually a
contribution at all for the purpose of the tax rules applying to the scheme
(PTM146600).
Contributors to registered pension schemes obtain tax relief on contributions they make
into the scheme and the scheme is exempt from tax on the income from, or gains made on
the disposal of, investments held by the scheme. Also, certain lump sums paid under the
scheme are exempt from income tax. These tax reliefs and exemptions are given by the
Government to encourage saving for an income in retirement.
To protect the integrity of these tax reliefs and exemptions, the tax rules distinguish
between authorised payments and unauthorised payments when a payment is made by a
registered pension scheme to or in respect of a person who is, or was, a member of the
scheme and also, in the case of a registered pension scheme that is an occupational
pension scheme, to or in respect of a person who is, or was, a sponsoring employer.
These same principles apply, equally, when a registered pension scheme is treated as
making a payment where that payment is made under or in connection with an investment
acquired with funds that have been held for the purpose of a registered pension scheme.
Despite putting in all appropriate checks and balances within an administration system,
errors by administrators of a pension scheme or by the scheme’s bank may still occur
which could result in an inadvertent payment being made, or the receipt of a contribution
into the scheme, that was not intended. Equally, errors could occur as a result of incorrect
information or late information being given to the scheme, such as by, or in respect of, a
member or the employer of a member or by a member’s or employer’s bank.
The facts and circumstances of each payment from, or to, a registered pension scheme
will determine whether or not that payment out, or payment in, is an unauthorised payment
or a contribution to the scheme. However, in certain circumstances, an inadvertent
payment caused by a genuine error would not be regarded as an unauthorised payment or
a contribution into the scheme, as the case may be.
8

CAS-119011-R3F8
Promptly rectified genuine ‘payment’ errors that are not unauthorised payments
An inadvertent payment made in the following circumstances will not be an unauthorised
payment:
• the payment is made in genuine error, such that there was no intention to make a
payment to that extent or at all, and
• the erroneous payment is spotted by someone involved with the management of
the scheme (or the recipient of the payment or the recipient’s adviser might have
brought the matter to the attention of the scheme managers), and
• the error is rectified as soon as reasonably possible.
There is no requirement for the scheme administrator to report a payment made in these
circumstances as an unauthorised payment, as the payment is not an unauthorised
payment for the purpose of the tax rules relating to registered pension schemes.
9

CAS-119011-R3F8
Appendix Two
PTM146600 - Other authorised payments: genuine errors: “contributions” to a
pension scheme that are not contributions
Introduction
Section 279(2) Finance Act 2004
Ordinarily, the tax rules limit the circumstances under which a contribution paid into a
registered pension scheme by, or on behalf of, a member or an employer can be refunded.
There are a few specific exceptions:
Specific member contributions that might be refunded
The value of contributions paid by, or on behalf of, a member (not including contributions
paid in respect of a member by the member’s employer) can be refunded if the payment
meets the conditions for:
• a refund of excess contributions lump sum (see PTM045000), or
• a short service refund lump sum (see PTM045000).
Specific employer contributions that might be refunded
Where contributions have been paid by a sponsoring employer to an occupational pension
scheme, excess amounts can be refunded if the payment is an authorised surplus
payment -see PTM145100.
Administration errors
However, if, as part of the day to day administration of the pension scheme, the scheme
receives contributions from (or on behalf of) a member or an employer in genuine error,
the repayment to the payer of the sums inadvertently received by the scheme will not be
an unauthorised payment. This is because the scheme was not entitled to the
contributions under its rules. The contributions are not therefore held for the purposes of
the scheme. So a return of the contributions to the payer is not a payment (either
authorised or unauthorised) for the purposes of Part 4 of Finance Act 2004 as they fall
outside the definition in Section 279(2).
Statutory ‘cooling off’ periods
Where, in respect of a registered pension scheme:
• a member pays contributions to the scheme, and
• the member subsequently changes his or her mind about the payment of those
contributions under a statutory ‘cooling off’ period, and
• those contributions are returned to the member
• that repayment will not be an unauthorised member payment.
10

CAS-119011-R3F8
Similarly, if a transfer is made to another registered pension scheme and the member is
entitled to change their mind under a statutory cooling-off provision, the repayment of the
transfer to the original registered pension scheme will not be regarded as an unauthorised
payment.
Taxation position
Any tax relief that a scheme administrator has claimed on contributions erroneously paid
under relief at source arrangements (PTM044220) must be repaid to HMRC. (The short
time span for statutory cooling off makes it less likely in that circumstance).
This repayment may be done by adjustment to the next claim made to HM Revenue &
Customs (HMRC) or alternatively by direct payment to HMRC.
Similarly, any tax relief that might have been given under net pay arrangement
(PTM044230) or by a claim (PTM044240) must be rectified by ensuring that no relief is
given or claimed in respect of any payments that, eventually, are not contributions.
The same would also apply in the case of any erroneous employer contributions.
11

CAS-119011-R3F8
Appendix Three
SIPP - Key Features Document
What happens if I exceed the Annual Allowance or Money Purchase Annual Allowance?
If you exceed the Annual Allowance, you may be able to carry forward any unused
allowance from the three previous tax years ("Carry Forward"). To take advantage of Carry
Forward, you must have been a member (even if no Contributions were made) of a UK
registered pension scheme for the tax year(s) in question. The amount available to carry
forward will be the difference between the Annual Allowance for the year in question and
the sum paid in that year to all of your pension schemes.
If the total pension contributions paid across all your pension schemes for the tax year
(including any amount carried forward form previous years), exceed your available Annual
Allowance, then you will be liable for a tax charge on the excess. The charge is based on
your marginal income tax rate (i.e. the highest rate at which you pay tax on your income).
If you are subject to the reduced money purchase annual allowance, you will not be able to
Carry Forward any unused allowance from previous years.

title: The Peoples Pension (CAS-112374-Z6S9)
text:
CAS-112374-Z6S9
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr L
Scheme The Peoples Pension (the Scheme)
Respondents Morson Limited (the Employer)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The sequence of events is not in dispute, so I have only set out the key points.
On 26 October 2016, Mr L began his employment with the Employer as a contractor
working for a third-party client (the Client).
Mr L’s contract of employment, signed on 26 October 2021, stated:-
“Subject to clause 4.3 the Company shall pay the Service Provider (employee)
for all hours worked, whether or not the Company has received payment from
the Client for such hours. The Company shall not make payment for hours not
worked.” (Clause 4.2) See Appendix One.
1

CAS-112374-Z6S9
In January 2017, Mr L was enrolled into the Scheme following a 12-week
postponement period1.
On 4 August 2023, Mr L contacted the Employer over concerns that when his weekly
timesheets were not approved by the Client, despite being submitted on time, this led
to Mr L missing out on relevant pension contributions. Mr L believed this affected the
weeks of 27 January 2023, 12 June 2023 and 21 July 2023.
On 7 August 2023, the Employer responded to Mr L and confirmed that it had passed
this issue to the contractor care team for advice.
On 7 August 2023, Mr L contacted the Employer and said that the issue went back to
2021.
On 9 August 2023, the Employer was advised that the pension payments were
calculated based on the amount manually keyed into the system for that payment
period. There were no missing pension payments as the pension contribution was
calculated based on the higher and lower earnings thresholds as set by the Pensions
Regulator (TPR) for the 2023/24 tax year (these thresholds were the same in
2022/23). The only way to avoid any perceived issue in the future was for timesheets
to be submitted and approved within the allocated timeframe.
On 9 August 2023, Mr L responded to the Employer asking what “amount was keyed
in” and what the higher and lower thresholds were. Mr L believed he was being
financially disadvantaged due to the Client’s system not working properly and due to
managers not being available or not approving the timesheets within the necessary
time limits. Mr L also raised the issue that onsite Wi-Fi did not always allow
timesheets to be submitted on time. Mr L did not want this to be an ongoing issue as
he was due to be offsite frequently towards the end of the year.
On 10 August 2023, the Employer explained that the lower weekly earnings threshold
was £120 and that the higher earnings threshold was £967. Meaning that no pension
deductions were made from the first £120 and that no additional deductions were
made above £967 per week.
On 11 August 2023, the Employer updated Mr L that further Client approvers could
be set up by one of Mr L’s current approvers. If multiple weeks of timesheets were
going through as one payment, then it is only that payment on which pension
contributions could be claimed.
On 9 September 2023, Mr L asked if it was possible for other people to be added as
timesheet approvers to avoid this issue. Or if managers can indicate that they are on
leave so that another approver is assigned in that situation.
1 Auto-enrolment postponement allows an employer to delay assessing and enrolling staff into its workplace
pension for up to three months. It can be applied to new staff, the duties start date, or when an employee
becomes eligible.
2

CAS-112374-Z6S9
On 14 October 2023, Mr L referred his complaint to the Pensions Ombudsman
(TPO).
On 10 November 2023, Mr L informed the Employer that he had taken his case to
TPO. Mr L requested that the missing pension payments be paid into the Scheme
where multiple weeks of timesheets had been treated as one payslip. Mr L said that
he was being financially penalised for issues beyond his control. Mr L was also
unhappy that the Client did not communicate managerial absences to him or put a
second approver in place. He was dissatisfied that there was often no Wi-Fi or mobile
phone reception onsite and there were issues with the Client payslip system when
submitting timesheets.
On 24 January 2025, Mr L provided TPO with a copy of his Morson employee
handbook and his employment contract which included the following:
“If the Service Provider fails to submit a relevant timesheet to the Company,
the Company in a timely fashion shall undertake such investigations as
appropriate to resolve the payment of the Fees for such hours completed by
the Service Provider.
Each timesheet must include any authorised expenses claimed (and, if the
Fees are calculated on an hourly half day or daily rate full details of the hours
services provided in relation the Project) must be in a form satisfactory to the
Company; and must be countersigned by an authorised representative of the
Client.
Such timesheets must not be submitted more frequently than on a weekly
basis and must be submitted within a period of not more than 3 months after
the work has been carried out.
Payment will be made by the Company (subject to factors beyond its control)
on the first Friday not less than 3 days after receipt of the relevant timesheet,
or as soon as practicable thereafter.” (Clause 4.3 - the employment contract
which can be found in Appendix One).
The Morson employee handbook included a ‘How do I submit my hours?’
section which explained that hours could be submitted via a timesheet
(Morson or client specific), via an Online Timesheet (OLTS) or via upload. This
section also included details of the Contractor Care Team who could be
contacted for support and that the employee’s Morson Recruitment Manager
could also be contacted for assistance.
On 22 May 2025, the Employer provided its formal response to Mr L’s complaint. In
summary it stated:
• Weekly payroll payments (pay periods) are aligned to tax weeks as per automatic
enrolment guidance based upon The Occupational and Personal Pensions
3

CAS-112374-Z6S9
Schemes (Automatic Enrolment) Regulations 2010 (the Regulations - which can
be found in Appendix Three).
• Regulation 3 (2) of the Regulations states that any qualifying earnings due in the
applicable pay reference period should be considered when calculating the
contributions due to the Scheme.
• Regulation 4 of the Regulations states that the pay reference period in the case of
a person who is paid their regular wage or salary by reference to a period of a
week is one week.
• Payroll is run and paid each week and when a timesheet is submitted or approved
late it will miss the relevant payroll processing, and it will be paid in the next pay
reference period.
• Pension calculations are made based on the pay reference period, and the total of
the multiple timesheets is used to calculate the pension contributions due based
on the relief at source qualifying earnings.
Summary of Mr L’s position:-
Adjudicator’s Opinion
Based on Regulation 4 of the Regulations states that Mr L’s pay reference period was
one week.
It was correct for the Employer to apply a single week’s qualifying earnings threshold
to the total amount payable in that pay reference period to determine Mr L’s pension
contributions regardless of the number of timesheets submitted. This was in
accordance with Regulation 4.
4

CAS-112374-Z6S9
Regulation 3 (2) of the Regulations states that qualifying earnings due in the
applicable pay reference period should be considered when calculating the
contributions due to the Scheme. As such the Employer acted reasonably when
considering the total amount payable in each pay reference period when working out
Mr L’s qualifying earnings and pension contributions. This was because the Employer
adopted a weekly pay reference period to calculate pension contributions in line with
Mr L’s employment contract.
The issues Mr L experienced appeared to be with the Client’s processing and
approval of Mr L’s timesheets. The Employer has acted within its obligations, and it
would not have been possible for the Employer to have received the timesheets
sooner. Although these technical issues may have been frustrating for Mr L it would
have been possible to submit timesheets later the same day or the next day in an
area with stronger Wi-Fi and or mobile phone signal. As a result of not acting in this
way, timesheets which could have been submitted in the previous week were
submitted alongside timesheets for the next relevant pay period.
Mr L provided his employment contract which states that the Employer must
investigate when timesheets have not been processed appropriately and that the
Employer must pay Mr L regardless of whether the Client had paid the Employer for
such hours. However, this does not relate to pension contributions which would need
to be calculated based on the number of hours worked and the set rate for those
hours. The Employer has complied with its obligations to pay Mr L once it received
timesheets from the Client.
In the Adjudicator’s view, it appears that there are numerous issues with the Client’s
timesheet system. Based on the available evidence Mr L appears to have made
efforts to ensure that his timesheets were submitted on time, but he was prevented
from doing so, in some instances, by technical issues.
Based on the available evidence it is likely that Mr L would have been able to submit
the affected timesheets sooner which may have resulted in earlier approval by the
Client. The Employer has acted within the Regulations on receiving the timesheets
from the Client and Mr L’s pension contributions have been paid accordingly.
Mr L did not accept the Adjudicator's Opinion, and the complaint was passed to me to
consider. Mr L submitted further comments in response to the Opinion. In summary
he said:-
• He is being financially penalised for things beyond his control. The online payment
system has faults, and his manager does not perform his duties in a prompt
manner or inform anybody when he is unavailable to sign off timesheets.
• Looking at the definition of pay refence period, it mentions time periods such as
weeks, months or annually with no mention of timesheets. As his timesheets show
end of week dates with hours worked it is clear he worked these weeks earning a
qualifying amount which attracts a pension payment.
5

CAS-112374-Z6S9
• Based on information from HMRC, it refers to total earnings being used to
calculate applicable pension contributions and having used the online calculator
for the last financial year there are large discrepancies not explained just by
missed time sheet deadlines.
I have considered Mr L’s further comments, but they do not change the outcome, I
agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
The Regulations state that all amounts payable in the pay reference period must be
included to calculate the qualifying earnings, this coincides with Regulation 3 (2). The
Employer was obliged to calculate the qualifying earnings based on the total amounts
payable in the pay reference period when calculating the pension contributions due to
the Scheme, regardless of the period the payment related to.
The Employer has made changes to its processes to allow for more timesheet
approval staff and avoid some of the issues faced by Mr L in the future. The other
issues raised by Mr L, such as the Client payslip system “not working” would be the
responsibility of the Client rather than to the Employer and in any case is
predominately an employment issue rather than a pension matter. I do note however
that some of the issues Mr L has mentioned, such as poor mobile phone reception or
a lack of onsite Wi-Fi, could have been mitigated by Mr L if he provided the relevant
information to the Client in another format, later the same day when he returned
home or on the following day or from a different location.
6

CAS-112374-Z6S9
I do not uphold Mr L’s complaint, and no further action is required by the Employer.
Camilla Barry
Deputy Pensions Ombudsman
06 July 2026
