title: IPS Pension Builder SIPP (CAS-106934-Y0N2)
text:
CAS-106934-Y0N2
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr Y
Scheme IPS Pension Builder SIPP (the SIPP)
Respondent James Hay Partnership (James Hay)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The sequence of events is not in dispute, so I have only set out the salient points. I
acknowledge there were other exchanges of information between all the parties.
1
James Hay Partnership

CAS-106934-Y0N2
2

CAS-106934-Y0N2
3

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• a completed Form 110 signed by Mr Y and the directors;
• a letter instructing it to release the assets to S&W signed by James Hay and Mr Y;
and
• a signed new client agreement which it was introducing from 1 January 2022, as
the transfer was unlikely to be completed by then.
• James Hay had asked for contingent transfers (that is all or nothing). However, it
could not accept such an instruction as the transfer process was outside its
control. If a bond transfer failed, then Vontobel would book it to a suspense
account and Kauders would ask it to book the asset back to the client account.
• It recommended that Mr Y send a list of assets to S&W and ask it to confirm its
ability to accept them. Mr Y duly did this, and S&W confirmed its ability to accept
all of the assets.
• There were inadequate instructions for the transfer of cash. GBP and USD were
held, and it needed the IBAN and BIC/Swift codes for the receiving bank for both.
4

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• Vontobel notified S&W that all the necessary documentation had been accepted,
and it was ready to deliver the assets. However, the balancing instruction S&W
had provided had not been signed by James Hay’s directors. In order to complete
the transfer, it needed the instruction signed by the three directors.
• James Hay emailed Mr Y. It said that it had not been informed that the balancing
instruction required signing by the directors. Asking the directors to sign this
instruction was possible, but they were located in different cities and rarely came
to its Salisbury office.
• Vontobel confirmed that it would check its requirements to see if FNZ signatures
could be utilised. If not, it said it would accept an individual James Hay director
signature so the balancing instruction could be scanned to one of the three
directors. Once signed, it could be couriered to Vontobel.
• On 16 December 2021, Vontobel was instructed to transfer his assets in the SIPP
to S&W. The assets were not received by S&W until 21 March 2022. On 11
October 2021, Kauders wrote to James Hay reminding it to sign the necessary
paperwork to regularise the account. Had this been actioned in a timely manner,
then it should have been possible to sell the bonds on 16 December 2021 for
£3,564,456.
• On 21 March 2022, the bonds were valued at £3,303,429 which was a reduction
in value of £260,977 [sic]. So, James Hay should refund him for this loss.
5

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• Its standard process was to provide, along with its instructions, copies of its own
legal documents with a certified copy of its current signatories list and power of
attorney for its various business entities. This legal documentation was included
with its instruction letter to S&W and included a power of attorney for James Hay
signed by two of its senior directors. Only in exceptional circumstances such as
Mr Y’s would it consider offering a concession and agree to complete other
businesses’ forms. Such a concession was agreed with Mr Y on 16 February
2022.
• It questioned the need for Form 110, which it said appeared to be a duplication of
effort. It also questioned why this form had to be signed by its CEO. Its servicing
operation was designed to provide the same fair and comparable level of service
to all its customers. It seemed unreasonable to expect the CEO of a business its
size to provide a wet signature to facilitate day to day administration on
customers’ accounts.
• It was unable to locate any instruction from Mr Y to encash part of the SIPP’s
assets; just to carry out an asset re-registration between his Swiss portfolio held
with Kauders and S&W.
• The asset value dates used by Mr Y were between 16 December 2021 and 21
March 2022. However, no assets were sold during this period, so such a loss did
not occur.
• The reason for the drop in asset value during this time was market fluctuations
and not due to its actions. Equally the value could have increased in this time. Mr
Y’s assets were held during this time in a discretionary investment portfolio. He
could have arranged to encash any holdings at any point in parallel with the asset
re-registration between Kauders and S&W. This decision was solely his as the
SIPP investor.
• The time taken to carry out the in-specie transfer was only due to the inflexible
requirements of Vontobel in only accepting wet signatures from senior directors
including its CEO. Further time was wasted by Vontobel not being clear as to what
it wanted.
• Mr Y’s complaint was perhaps best characterised as his expectations not
matching with the service James Hay could reasonably offer. This did not mean
that its service was improper or should be any different.
Following the complaint being referred to The Pensions Ombudsman (TPO), Mr Y
and James Hay made further submissions that have been summarised below.
Mr Y said:-
6

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• Kauders’ decision to move to Switzerland and to relocate his assets would appear
to have resulted in a fundamental change to its administrative requirements.
James Hay and Kauders should have reassessed the nature of their relationship
and highlighted any possible pitfalls to their clients before they arose. At no time
was he advised that his circumstances were exceptional and that a concession
would be required from James Hay for what appeared to be a routine transaction.
Had he known this at the time he would have made alternative arrangements.
• He is claiming a financial loss of 50% of the reduction in the value of his SIPP’s
bonds sustained between 16 December 2021 and 21 March 2022. The reduction
in value was £260,971 resulting in a loss to him of £130,485.50.
• He would have sold more than 50% of his bonds as he was becoming increasingly
uneasy as to the direction of the bond market. However, by the time S&W
received the portfolio from Kauders, he considered it too late.
James Hay said:-
• Information had first been requested in relation to Vontobel’s requirements in the
middle of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The request was not progressed at
the time as it was not practical for it to do so. The request was initially just for
Vontobel to update its records, and not for a transaction. Even if it had taken
action in September/October 2020, a new Form 110 would have been needed in
December 2021 as the mandate would have been out of date due to its directors
having changed between October 2020 and December 2021.
• While the in-specie transfer was being carried out between Kauders and S&W,
there was no restriction for Mr Y to continue selling assets. This was the whole
point of an in-specie transfer, designed to not disturb investment strategy during
the transfer.
• The key issue that Mr Y complained about, regarding not being able to sell his
bonds holding, does not lie with James Hay but between Mr Y and his investment
manager at the time, Kauders.
• Furthermore, Mr Y specifically complained he could have sold his bonds on 16
December 2021. However, at that point, it had only received Mr Y’s instruction to
transfer the assets and close the Kauders account. The transfer to S&W would
have never been completed by 16 December 2021, which means James Hay
cannot be held responsible for the specific loss Mr Y is claiming.
• It had no record of receiving any communication making it aware that Mr Y
intended to sell any of his bonds on completion of the in-specie transfer. He had
mentioned that he had concerns about market fluctuations when the in-specie
transfer became protracted, but nothing more.
7

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• invoice 1061349 for £810.00 covering administration charges from February 2020
to January 2021;
• invoice 1061487 for £114.00 covering investment manager / stockbroker account
charges from February 2021 to January 2022; and
• invoice 1061240 for £194.40 covering income drawdown charges from February
2021 to January 2022.
“If we do not receive any communication within 14 days from the date of this
letter, then in line with the product terms and conditions, we will arrange for a
sale from the largest value asset in the plan to cover the outstanding fees and
any associated charges.”
• Mr Y said that the Letter seemed to be fraudulent and poorly worded. He advised
that he had been in contact with UBS’ and the police’s fraud departments. Mr Y
maintained that he had no outstanding fees.
8

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• James Hay told Mr Y that the Letter was genuine. It confirmed that the fees were
correct and outstanding, and it provided further details of what the fees related to.
• James Hay told Mr Y that it would take no further action.
• invoice 1066583 for £907.20 covering renewal fees;
• invoice 1066670 for £120.00 covering investment manager fees;
• invoice 1066538 for £68.40 covering external bank account fees; and
• invoice 1066637 for £205.20 covering annual drawdown fees.
9

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• It apologised that Mr Y’s complaint of 26 October 2021 had not been referred to its
customer relations team.
• Invoices were raised against his SIPP in February 2021 in the same way as in
previous years. A reminder letter was then sent on 5 September 2021, but they
remain unpaid. Mr Y had suggested that these invoices had been paid by cheque
in August 2021. However, this payment was in respect of different invoices.
• The sum due consisted of the three invoices dated 15 February 2021, together
with a 52p sum outstanding on an invoice raised on 18 August 2021 that had been
partially paid.
• It noted that Mr Y usually paid his SIPP fees soon after they were due by cheque.
It was not sure why this did not happen in this instance.
• It had followed its standard process for when fees were outstanding for some
time. A letter was sent to UBS requesting that it send the necessary amount to
clear the fees due. It was not sure why Mr Y and UBS had treated this as fraud.
• There was nothing to suggest issues with its administration, so no compensation
was due.
• Section 16.6 of the SIPP’s terms and conditions (the T&Cs) stated that: “subject
to our requirements and methods of payment as we may decide, you can pay
charges and costs personally instead of deducting them from your SIPP”. He
10

CAS-106934-Y0N2
confirmed that this was the arrangement that was in place for him. He questioned
why no one at James Hay telephoned him if there was a problem.
• James Hay’s letter to UBS of 10 October 2021 had suspicious signatures. These
signatures did not appear on the copy of the letter that James Hay submitted to
TPO, which was alarming.
• Its invoices had been sent to Mr Y’s home address since 2006. It acknowledged
that, historically, Mr Y had sent it cheques rather than paying the fees from within
the SIPP.
• It did not understand why it had agreed during the telephone call on 22 October
2021 to waive the three fees. The fees were raised in accordance with its terms
and conditions and the relevant charges schedule. They were also raised at the
correct time and invoices were sent to the correct address. It would only waive
fees when it had done something wrong which was not the case here.
• Section 16.5 of the T&Cs stated that it reserved the right to sell investments to pay
its charges.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
• By their nature, in-specie transfers could be time consuming due to the
complexities involved in assessing all the assets and ensuring that the receiving
party was able to accept them.
• It was not unreasonable for in-specie transfers to be given less urgency than
transfers involving the sale and purchase of assets. By its very nature, the timing
of an in-specie transfer did not involve a risk to the value of the underlying assets.
• In the instance of Mr Y’s SIPP, Vontobel had a number of due diligence
requirements that James Hay had to comply with. These requirements were
specific to Mr Y’s SIPP.
11

CAS-106934-Y0N2
The fee administration complaint
12

CAS-106934-Y0N2
“We reserve the right to sell investments in order to pay our charges,
expenses, third party charges and costs (including Adviser Charges), tax
charges, levies or fees that may have been reasonably incurred in the
administration of your SIPP and the investments held within it. Although we
reserve this right we shall be under no obligation to exercise it and it remains
your responsibility to comply with clause 16.4 above.”
13

CAS-106934-Y0N2
• terminated his relationship with Kauders; or, more likely
• moved to a provider that had robust systems in place to deal with investment
managers based in Switzerland.
• It had to agree to another concession to enable it to complete other businesses’
forms. This was further evidence that James Hay’s processes were not sufficiently
robust to satisfy the fund manager’s requirements.
• James Hay said that it seemed unreasonable to expect the CEO of a business its
size to facilitate day-to-day administration. However, this did not alter what was
required. If it felt this was unreasonable, why did it agree to a concession in
December 2013 allowing the business relationship with Kauders and La Roche to
continue? Although the custodian at the time was different, the potential
requirements of Swiss law, and how these might be at odds with James Hay’s
processes, appear not to have been considered.
• For James Hay to state that it was unable to locate any instruction from Mr Y to
encash part of the SIPP’s assets was incorrect. There was plenty of evidence to
the contrary, a sample of emails sent to James Hay being provided:-
o An email from Mr Y on 29 January 2022, in which he chased the signing of
Form 101, saying that: “… it is extremely urgent to recover our US Treasuries
from Vontobel as the market is falling away very quickly.”
14

CAS-106934-Y0N2
o An email from Mr Y on 4 February 2022, in which he said: “… it appears that
trying to obtain our US Treasuries and bonds from Vontobel, the portfolio has
dropped approximately £350,000. Time really is of the essence as we need
our exit strategy underway. This delay has proved to be very expensive. I can
only hope that the 101 form has been correctly signed and will be with
Vontobel in the very near future …”
o An email from S&W on 9 February 2022, in which it said: “[Mr Y] and I are
watching the falling bond market anxiously, and the portfolio cannot be
changed until this step is completed, so we are desperately keen to keep this
moving as quickly as possible.”
o An email from S&W on 16 February 2022, in which it said: “We are anxious to
complete the transfer urgently because the portfolio cannot be changed while
it is held by Vontobel and it is invested in government bonds which are falling
in value. I estimate that the portfolio has lost £255,050 in value since 10th
December, of that a £134,161 fall in value has arisen while James Hay have
been arranging signatures.” James Hay responded: “Completely understand
the urgency.”
• It was disingenuous of James Hay to suggest that Vontobel was inflexible and
wasted time by not being clear about what it wanted. It was James Hay that
wasted time, in addition to being incapable of satisfying the requirements of a
Swiss custodian in a timely manner. This, despite agreeing a special concession
to deal with those requirements in December 2013.
• Mr Y accepts that his expectations did not match the service that James Hay
offered. He had no idea that James Hay’s service, particularly with regard to its
dealings with a Swiss custodian, was likely to be in any way lacking. He submits
that, with no knowledge that a special concession had been necessary to maintain
the business relationship with Switzerland, it was unreasonable of James Hay to
suggest otherwise.
The Adjudicator considered it not unreasonable for in-specie transfers to be given
less urgency than transfers involving the sale and purchase of assets. Mr Y did not
agree. He was trying desperately to arrange the sale and purchase of assets but
could not do so as a result of James Hay’s inefficiency. Consequently, and against
his better judgment, an in-specie transfer had to be dealt with first, so the proposed
sale and purchase could proceed. Speed was key to such transactions.
15

CAS-106934-Y0N2
In relation to the fee administration part of Mr Y’s complaint, one of the invoices
looked so suspicious that UBS referred the document to its Fraud Department. Mr Y
was caused considerable concern in seeking to understand the position. James Hay
acknowledged that undue stress had resulted and it was this that led to an offer of
monetary recompense, by writing off any outstanding fees. Mr Y accepted this offer.
The Adjudicator’s view was that James Hay’s failure to deliver on that undertaking
was an acceptable way to do business. An offer had been made and accepted, and
Mr Y’s view is that this constitutes a contract.
It had no ongoing relationship with Kauders. Kauders was appointed by Mr Y to act
as his investment manager in relation to his pension investments.
As a regulated business and approved pension provider, it has business policies and
standard procedures in place to ensure it fulfilled its obligations and to provide a
consistent and reliable service to its customers. It could go outside of these policies
and procedures provided they did not breach regulations, and they were feasible
requests that did not have a detrimental impact on other customers. These occasions
were referred to as “concessions”. It did not then consider that customer’s SIPP to be
special or outside of the scope of its normal policies and procedures.
It did not ordinarily allow customers to open investment manager accounts that were
not regulated by the FCA. However, Mr Y already had an investment management
account with Kauders at the time it chose to move its business to Switzerland. The
nature of Mr Y’s SIPP also meant that he was in charge of his investment decisions,
and so James Hay only acted as the receiver and transmitter of customer
instructions. Between December 2011 and February 2012, Mr Y and Kauders
provided it with various documents that needed to be completed and signed in order
to open the new account with La Roche. Given that the account would come under
16

CAS-106934-Y0N2
Swiss financial regulations, it allowed the account to be opened. It apologised that it
had previously confirmed that a concession was not granted until December 2013; in
fact, this was just when the concession was formally noted for its internal records.
At the time that it allowed the Swiss account to be opened, there was no indication
that there would be any issues in being able to provide instructions to the investment
manager. It understood that Mr Y would be able to provide investment instructions
directly to Kauders and withdrawals from the account would be authorised by Mr Y
together with two authorised signatories of the trustees. It could not have foreseen
the issues that occurred ten years later.
Its SIPP customers exercise their choice to open investment manager accounts with
many different companies. These companies have individual requirements that can
differ from one another, and it was not feasible for James Hay to have an established
procedure for dealing with each of these. It has a general procedure in place for
providing instructions to investment managers which was widely accepted. However,
there are times when investment managers respond with further requirements that
need to be met before they will act on instruction. So, it frequently went outside its
general procedure to fulfil the further requirements, which usually happens without
incident.
The issues that occurred with Mr Y’s in-specie transfer were down to the unusual
nature of Vontobel’s requirements. Vontobel were not the custodian in 2012 when it
allowed the Kauders account to be transferred to Switzerland, and it had no control
over the change in the custodian from La Roche to Vontobel later on. However,
Vontobel’s requirements were not insurmountable, but they took time to fulfil as
original signatures were required from a number of James Hay’s executives. In
addition, its requirements were not all clearly presented at the start of the process.
In 2020, Vontobel contacted James Hay to obtain signatures from its company
executives. However, it was not able to meet this request due to the COVID-19
pandemic and lockdowns in the UK. This had no bearing on what happened in 2022
as its company executives had changed since 2020, and so it would always have
been necessary to satisfy Vontobel’s requirements again.
It cannot agree that it could have foreseen or prevented what transpired in relation to
the in-specie transfer.
It did not deny that Mr Y mentioned, on a number of occasions, his concerns with the
changing markets or that it was suggested that investments might be sold following
completion of the in-specie transfer. However, it could not find any evidence that it
told Mr Y that he could not sell any of the investments either before the in-specie
transfer commenced or while the transfer process was on-going. If Mr Y had asked
for an investment to be sold it would have transmitted this instruction to the
investment manager. It was Kauders that told Mr Y that it would not permit any sales,
which is why he chose to go down the route of an in-specie transfer.
17

CAS-106934-Y0N2
It does not treat in-specie transfers with any less urgency than cash transfers, so this
was not a consideration during the process.
Ombudsman’s decision
18

CAS-106934-Y0N2
In the response on Mr Y’s behalf to the Adjudicator’s Opinion, reference is made to
the considerable concern he was caused by an invoice issued by James Hay that he
viewed as being suspicious. While I acknowledge that this was a cause of distress for
Mr Y, it was something that could have easily been validated by contacting James
Hay, as UBS did eventually do.
Mr Y also referred to the Adjudicator taking the view that James Hay’s failure to
deliver on the ‘undertaking’ made to Mr Y in the telephone conversation on 22
October 2021 was an acceptable way to do business. I do not agree that this is what
the Adjudicator said. In his Opinion, the Adjudicator identified this as being
maladministration on the part of James Hay. This was the primary reason that the
Adjudicator upheld Mr Y’s complaint in part, stating that James Hay should pay Mr Y
£500 for the distress and inconvenience he had suffered. I find this to have been a
reasonable approach given the circumstances.
Mr Y referred to an offer being made during this telephone conversation that he
accepted. He maintained that this constituted a contract. I have not been able to
identify the necessary elements for a contract to exist; that is, offer, acceptance,
consideration and an intention to enter into legal relations of a contractual nature. In
particular, I cannot see that there was any intention on the part of James Hay’s call
handler to enter into a legal relationship with Mr Y. In particular, I note that James
Hay continued to chase for payment of the invoices after that call and, clearly, had
not agreed to waive the outstanding amount. Furthermore, James Hay did not collect
the unpaid sum from Mr Y’s holdings, as it was entitled to do under the T&Cs, until
further attempts were made to seek settlement. Nonetheless, I do agree with my
Adjudicator that the call constitutes maladministration.
19

CAS-106934-Y0N2
Directions
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman
30 June 2026
20

title: Fidelity SIPP (CAS-88367-R8K8)
text:
CAS-88367-R8K8
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr N
Scheme Fidelity SIPP (the SIPP)
Respondent
Fidelity International (Fidelity)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The SIPP is a Self-Invested Personal Pension. Mr N was the SIPP member and one
of his chosen investments was the Fund, held as part of the SIPP. Invesco was the
provider and the Manager of the Fund.
The Terms and Conditions of the SIPP (the SIPP Terms) under clause 1.2
“Communicating with you” stated “Our service is primarily an online service for which
you will need to register. If you do so we will, by default, send most documents to
your secure online mailbox.”
Under clause 4b the SIPP Terms said, “In the case of mandatory Corporate Actions
(i.e. those where you cannot choose the Outturn), the notification may be provided to
you after any Outturn has been credited to your account.”
1
Fidelity International

CAS-88367-R8K8
Fidelity’s online service included a section where a member was able to select their
preferences for how Fidelity communicated with them. This was in terms of how
documents were issued, as well as an option to select whether email notifications
were sent whenever a new document was issued or uploaded online. The email alert
option appeared as a tick box alongside the wording “Send out Email Notifications.”
Fidelity says the default position upon first registering for its online service was that
the email alert function was active.
Fidelity says that where it had a regulatory obligation to do so, email notifications
would always be issued, irrespective of a member’s selected preferences. It has
confirmed that it did not send email alerts or email copies for correspondence related
to corporate actions.
At the time of the events that are the subject of Mr N’s complaint, his communication
preferences were different to the default, and all documents were issued online only
and the option for email alerts was not active.
Fidelity says that the email alert option had been “turned off completely” by Mr N in
2014, and that it remained unchanged until he turned it back on in 2022.
Fidelity says that Mr N edited his communication preferences on 6 August 2020, but
that no changes were made to the email alert function at that time.
On 30 November 2021, Fidelity received notification from Invesco that the Fund
would be closed.
In February 2022, Fidelity received further correspondence from Invesco, confirming
the Fund was closing. It uploaded a letter to Mr N’s online account on 19 February
2022 to let him know (the Notification). This letter appeared in Mr N’s inbox with the
narrative of “Miscellaneous Letter.”
The Notification explained that the Fund would close on 11 March 2022 and that if Mr
N wanted to take action, he should submit instructions to Fidelity by 3 March 2022. It
said the alternative option was to “do nothing” and the investment would be moved to
cash after the closure date.
Fidelity did not receive any instructions or contact from Mr N in this period in respect
of the Fund, and it was subsequently moved into cash (in the amount of £37,363.99).
On 20 March 2022, Mr N raised a complaint with Fidelity. He had noticed the drop in
the value of the SIPP and became aware of the closure of the Fund. Fidelity’s
response was issued on 19 May 2022, and it did not uphold Mr N’s complaint.
2

CAS-88367-R8K8
On 22 May 2022, Mr N responded to Fidelity to explain why he did not agree with its
position. Further exchanges between Fidelity and Mr N followed and through its
further investigations, Fidelity identified it had not made Mr N aware of the notification
it had received from Invesco on 30 November 2021. It said it should have done so,
apologised and made Mr N an offer of £100 for non-financial injustice.
Mr N’s position
A summary of the submissions and comments provided by Mr N is set out below.
• Fidelity failed to adequately notify him that the Fund was closing. He was not
aware of it, and so was unable to take any action before it closed. By that time,
the Fund’s value had dropped significantly, and he had incurred financial loss in
the region of £30,000.
• Fidelity’s systems in terms of how it provided documents and how it set out the
available communication preferences was not fit for purpose and was misleading.
• The communication options were not clear and explicit in terms of explaining the
implications of each setting. For example, the options named as “online only” or
“post & online” were not clear to explain email alerts would not be sent. It was
reasonable for him to have understood the reference to online in those options to
include email and that copies of documents would be issued that way.
• When turning off email alerts he had assumed the alerts related to marketing
information. When changing preferences, no warning was given to advise he may
not receive notification for documents relating to corporate actions.
• He understood corporate actions would be included. It was not reasonable to
expect him to know what documents would be excluded from receiving alerts and
which documents would be classed as a regulatory document. Fidelity had a
responsibility to ensure important documents reached him and it had failed to do
so with the Notification.
• He understood his communication preference settings were made on the day he
registered for Fidelity’s online service. When reviewing those settings years later,
he would not have been aware that email alerts were opted out of. When he made
changes in August 2020 there was no information available on the relevant screen
to show that email alerts had been opted out of and were switched off. He was not
aware he would not receive email copies or email notification of important
documents, such as corporate actions. He should have received an email on this
occasion.
• He could not reasonably be expected to log into his account online each day and
to check whether any new documents had been uploaded. He did log in regularly,
but there was no indication of new messages on the initial home screen, and that
was a failure of Fidelity’s system.
3

CAS-88367-R8K8
• Fidelity’s delay in sending the notification it received in November 2021 was a
critical issue. He had been given a short period to act when Fidelity had been
aware of the closure of the Fund for three months before it informed him. He did
not agree with its view that he would not have taken action if he had known about
it earlier. He regularly logged in online to “check his position” and was a careful
and attentive investor.
Fidelity’s position
A summary of the submissions and comments provided by Fidelity is set out below.
4

CAS-88367-R8K8
Adjudicator’s Opinion
Mr N’s complaint was considered by one of our Adjudicators who concluded that no
further action was required by Fidelity. The Adjudicator’s findings are summarised
below.
The Adjudicator explained his findings did not provide any comment on the matter of
how Fidelity managed Mr N’s complaint or how long it took to respond to him. He said
that specific issue had not been accepted for investigation.
The Adjudicator confirmed it was his view that Fidelity had issued the Notification to
Mr N in an appropriate way, and in accordance with Mr N’s own directions in terms of
how it should communicate with him. On this point, the Adjudicator said the evidence
showed Mr N’s communication preferences at the time of the Notification were that he
should receive documents “online only” and the option to receive email alerts had
been switched off. He noted that the SIPP Terms stated “most documents” issued by
Fidelity would be sent to Mr N through the inbox associated with his online account.
The Adjudicator also said he agreed with Fidelity’s position that it was only required to
provide email notifications to Mr N regarding regulatory documents and that this did
not include corporate actions. He added that he considered Fidelity did not have any
responsibility to send the Notification to Mr N in a way other than email.
The Adjudicator highlighted that Mr N had not disputed the communication
preferences held by Fidelity at the time of the Notification or that he had made
changes to them, including de-activating email alerts. In addition, Mr N had said his
selections were made when he first registered for Fidelity’s online service and had not
disputed the fact no changes were made to them between 2014 and the issuing of
the Notification.
In respect of Mr N’s comments that it was reasonable for him to have expected to
receive email copies or email notification of important documents and that the options
for communication preferences were misleading, the Adjudicator did not agree.
5

CAS-88367-R8K8
He explained it was his view that the preferences were clear and, especially so with
regards to email alerts. He said these were explicit to show the option to receive them
when a document was issued was either active or not. The Adjudicator said he had
focused on the email alert option because it had been Mr N’s decision to turn it off
and it was that decision that resulted in Fidelity not sending him an email about the
Notification.
The Adjudicator explained that in his opinion, the preferences were sufficiently clear
to have allowed Mr N to recognise that documents would be provided to his online
account only, if he chose the option “online only.” He also referenced the SIPP Terms
again, to note that these stated that this would be the case for most documents.
In addition, the Adjudicator considered that Mr N could have raised a query with
Fidelity at any time, if he was unclear about any of the preferences and how
documents would be sent or how he would be notified depending on the selections
he made. He said that was both when Mr N first made his selections and when he
made changes in August 2020. The Adjudicator noted there was no evidence to show
that Mr N had raised any such queries with Fidelity prior to the Notification being sent.
In respect of the changes Mr N made to his communication preferences in August
2020 and his comment that no information was present about the email alert function
at that time, the Adjudicator did not consider that to be a material issue. He said that
was because the key event was when Mr N deactivated email alerts and that had
already happened by August 2020.
The Adjudicator agreed with Fidelity’s position that it was Mr N’s responsibility to
check his inbox for any new documents, and he said that was not least because of
the communication preferences Mr N had chosen.
The Adjudicator explained that he considered Fidelity’s apology and its offer of £100
for non-financial injustice to be appropriate, regarding its failure to make Mr N aware
of the notification received in November 2021.
He said this was because Fidelity did not provide any commitment in the SIPP Terms,
with regards to a timescale for notifying a SIPP member of a corporate action. On this
point, he highlighted that under clause 4b the SIPP terms said that for mandatory
corporate actions, notification could be provided after the “outturn”, so for a fund
closure, it could occur after the fund had already been moved into cash.
The Adjudicator noted that Fidelity did provide the Notification to Mr N before the
relevant deadline for him to act; it was uploaded to his online account on 19 February
2022, and the deadline was 3 March 2022. He said that in his opinion, that period
was reasonable and long enough for Mr N to have identified the document in his
online account and to have provided any instructions to Fidelity. He said that in his
view, the fact Mr N became aware of the Notification after the relevant deadline, was
not a consequence of Fidelity’s actions.
6

CAS-88367-R8K8
Fidelity accepted the Adjudicator’s Opinion and did not provide any additional
comments.
Mr N did not accept the Opinion, and he provided his additional comments. These
were largely to reiterate the points he had already made. His further comments are
nonetheless summarised below: -
• His views remained unchanged. It was hard to accept that the onus was on him, a
non-sophisticated financial investor, to know that emails related to Corporate
Actions would not be included in regulatory messages and he would not receive
separate notification.
• Fidelity's systems were poorly designed and not fit for purpose. By ticking the opt-
out box, he would have had to log in weekly (as he was doing), then navigate to
the messaging section of the system to see if any new messages were waiting.
There was no visual indication when logging in that a message needed attention.
If that had been provided, he would have very likely been able to act in time.
• Fidelity admitted its mistake that the Notification was issued very late. It should
have recognised it would have been “good customer care” to send it directly to
him rather than upload it to its system. He had less than a week to act.
• The offer made by Fidelity of £100 was not sufficient, given the magnitude of the
loss he suffered.
• Fidelity had shared additional information with The Pensions Ombudsman that
was not relevant, about his non-pension holdings. This was at least a breach of
data protection and likely done to influence the outcome of his complaint, to
suggest he could afford the loss amount claimed.
As Mr N did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion, the complaint was passed to me to
consider. I have reviewed the post Opinion comments provided by Mr N, but they do
not change the outcome. I agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
Mr N complained that Fidelity did not adequately notify him of the closure of the Fund.
My Determination does not provide any finding on the other matters raised by Mr N,
in respect of Fidelity’s handling of his complaint and his comments about the
information shared by Fidelity and data protection. These issues were not accepted
for investigation. I would also note that complaints about the latter would be dealt with
by the Information Commissioner's Office.
7

CAS-88367-R8K8
Mr N has not disputed that he made the decision to deactivate email alerts or that he
selected the option that he should receive correspondence “online only.” Ultimately,
he received communications in the manner he had, proactively, requested. However,
he contends the differing options presented to him were misleading and has
effectively said that, in the circumstances, Fidelity should have done more to ensure
he was aware of the closure of the Fund in time.
In terms of how Fidelity issued notification of the closure of the Fund to Mr N, I agree
with the Adjudicator’s view that it was appropriate for it to have done so by uploading
it to his online account. That was in accordance with the instructions it had received
from Mr N, when he selected his communication preferences.
I do not agree the communication preferences presented to Mr N were misleading. I
consider that when selecting the option of “online only” and turning off the email alert
function, Mr N should reasonably have known he would receive correspondence to
his online account directly and at times without any additional form of notification.
It was disappointing that Fidelity did not contact Mr N following the initial notification it
received from Invesco. However, I agree with the Adjudicator’s view here, and I too
am satisfied that the period of time provided to Mr N was reasonable and sufficient for
him to have taken action. It was his responsibility to monitor his account regularly and
taking into account the overall circumstances, I do not consider Fidelity is responsible
for Mr N becoming aware of the Notification beyond the specified deadline.
Therefore, I do not uphold Mr N’s complaint.
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman
29 June 2026
8

title: Medical Defence Union Pension and Life Assurance Scheme (CAS-93357-D7V7)
text:
CAS-93357-D7V7
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr E
Scheme Medical Defence Union Pension and Life Assurance Scheme (the
Scheme)
Respondents Aon
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The sequence of events is not in dispute, so I have only set out the salient points. I
acknowledge there were other exchanges of information between all the parties.
On 7 February 2022, Aon sent Mr E a retirement pack (the retirement pack)
showing his pension benefits with a retirement date of 1 April 2022. The fund value
was quoted as £107,927. The options available to Mr E were to purchase an annuity
or claim payment of a taxable lump sum. The retirement pack included the following:
“Estimates of your benefit options available in the Scheme are summarised
below. You'll find more details on the following pages, as well as an
explanation of terms in the 'Finding out more' section. We've colour-coded
your options to make them easier to find. The different options have different
features, rates of payment and possible tax implications. These figures aren't
guaranteed due to the changing nature of investment markets. The value of
your fund can go down as well as up.”
Mr E says he completed and returned the enclosed retirement forms (the retirement
forms) to Aon soon after receiving the retirement pack, but that when he did not hear
from Aon by the “end of March” he contacted it again.

CAS-93357-D7V7
On 22 March 2022, Aon received a notification from Mr E’s Independent Financial
Advisor (IFA) stating that he intended to purchase an annuity through Legal &
General (L&G). The IFA also asked a number of questions in relation to Mr E’s
membership of the Scheme. At this point Aon says it had not yet received Mr E’s
completed retirement forms.
On 1 April 2022, Mr E reached his chosen retirement date.
On 8 April 2022, Aon sent documentation stating that the fund value was £107,927.
On 13 April 2022, Mr E called Aon to request that it reissue the retirement pack,
which it did immediately by email.
On the same day, the IFA called Aon to request a transfer out pack to facilitate the
transfer of funds to L&G.
On 19 April 2022, Aon received Mr E’s completed retirement forms notifying Aon that
he wished to use the entirety of his fund to purchase an annuity with L&G. After
reviewing the retirement forms, Aon noted that Mr E had not completed the Lifetime
Allowance1 (LTA) section.
On 25 April 2022, Aon sent a transfer out pack to the IFA and Mr E, the fund value
was quoted as £104,354.13.
On 28 April 2022, Aon wrote to Mr E and asked that he complete the LTA section of
the retirement forms. Aon also called (the Call) Mr E regarding the transfer out pack
that had been issued and asked for clarity on whether he was hoping to purchase an
annuity with an external provider. Mr E notified Aon that he no longer wished to
purchase an annuity with L&G and was told that he would have to resubmit the
necessary forms to confirm this.
On 3 May 2022, the IFA notified Aon that Mr E wished to purchase an annuity with
Just. The IFA also raised a number of queries regarding Mr E’s membership of the
Scheme.
On 11 May 2022, Aon answered the IFA’s queries by email.
On 13 May 2022, Mr E and his IFA called Aon to confirm what documentation was
required by Aon to process Mr E’s retirement. Aon said that it required the completed
retirement forms indicating Mr E’s wish to purchase an annuity with Just.
On 19 May 2022, Aon received Mr E’s correctly completed retirement forms. It
subsequently disinvested the relevant funds which were received in the Scheme’s
account on 24 May 2022.
1
The lifetime allowance was a cap on the total value of pension savings an individual could accumulate across all registered pension
schemes without incurring a tax charge.
2

CAS-93357-D7V7
On 30 May 2022, Aon confirmed that the funds had been disinvested and that the
amount was £100,124. This was £7,802 less than Aon stated on 8 April 2022.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
Mr E’s complaint was considered by one of our Adjudicators who concluded that no
further action was required by Aon. The Adjudicator’s findings are summarised below:
She did not believe Aon have caused any delays in processing Mr E’s retirement. The
issue appears to have been that both Mr E and his IFA were chasing information and
corresponding with Aon concurrently. This resulted in overlapping requests which
delayed the retirement process.
Having reviewed the various exchanges between Mr E, the IFA and Aon there were
several instances where overlapping requests were made:
When Aon received Mr E’s first completed retirement forms on 19 April 2022, Aon
had noticed that Mr E had failed to complete the LTA section, and rightly requested
that he complete them again. It only took eight working days for Aon to make this
request. This was an acceptable timeframe.
The retirement packs and transfer packs were issued within Aon’s normal turnaround
times and when Mr E requested them to be reissued, they were provided in a timely
manner. There seems to have been a misunderstanding between the parties to this
3

CAS-93357-D7V7
complaint regarding the terminology being used. The main issue being around the
phrase “transfer.” There is a difference between transferring out of a pension
arrangement and transferring out in order to purchase annuity, both of which require
separate forms to be completed. So, confusion appears to have arisen when the
phrase transfer has been used without further qualification. This resulted in multiple
conflicting requests which in turn has delayed the retirement process.
There also seems to be a miscommunication between Mr E and his IFA as it seems
Mr E wished to purchase an annuity and had requested this initially and then his IFA
requested a transfer pack.
Mr E has expressed his frustration at Aon for issuing the transfer out pack. However,
it is important to note that Aon was acting on the request of Mr E’s IFA and any
confusion caused by this transfer out pack was quickly clarified with Mr E in the 28
April 2022 call. She therefore did not believe that issuing the transfer pack caused
any delays to Mr E’s retirement. In her opinion, the transfer out pack was issued
alongside the retirement pack and as Mr E wanted to purchase an annuity, he could
have simply discarded the transfer pack.
When Aon made the Call, Mr E had chosen to change who he wanted to purchase an
annuity with. In my opinion, this caused a delay as Aon did not receive the newly
completed retirement forms until 19 May 2022. Mr E claims he had chosen to change
his annuity option as he did not have faith that L&G could provide the retirement he
wanted and needed to change the provider to “survive.” Regardless of his reasons for
changing his preferred annuity provided it is without doubt this caused a delay in his
onward purchase of an annuity.
Upon receiving the completed retirement forms Aon disinvested the funds and paid
them to Just within eight working days, which is a relatively quick turnaround time to
process the administrational processes and then have the funds transferred over to
Just.
It is important to note that Aon’s retirement packs have the caveat as shown in
paragraph four, which clearly confirms that the values provided are an estimate and
that the value of the fund can go up or down. Therefore, in her opinion although the
retirement forms issued to Mr E in February and April 2022 seemed to be the same
value this did not automatically secure the figure. This was confirmed when the value
quoted in the transfer pack decreased, which was due to the volatile economic
market which was not within Aon’s control.
When Mr E decided to change the annuity provider this meant new forms were
required which in turn took more time. The amended forms were not received until 19
May 2022. It is unfortunate that the value decreased during this period, but this was
not caused by any delay by Aon.
Mr E did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion and the complaint was passed to me to
consider. Mr E provided his further comments which do not change the outcome. I
agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion and note the additional points raised Mr E.
4

CAS-93357-D7V7
Mr E’s Comments
He felt that the Adjudicator failed to take into account Aon causing him to “doubt” L&G
due to its confusion and he would not have changed provider if it were not for this.
He is dissatisfied that the Adjudicator claimed he “could have simply discarded the
transfer pack.” Aon sent duplicate copies of the transfer pack and insisted he should
complete them. He reiterated that he informed Aon several times this was incorrect,
but it would not listen and also insisted to his IFA that he should complete a transfer
pack and not the retirement pack. Therefore, Aon were the confused party and by
insisting he should complete the wrong forms, caused confusion and delay.
He does not accept the Adjudicators opinion that he only submitted fully completed
retirement forms on 19 May 2022. He actually submitted completed retirement forms
in February 2022, which Aon claim it did not receive. He provided evidence that he
sent the forms back via email, and he claims that if Aon had processed these forms
back in February 2022, then no doubts, or confusion would have arisen, and he
would not have doubted L&G despite Aon's connections with them. As such, no
delays would have occurred, and so no reduction in his annuity sum.
Ombudsman’s decision
Mr E complains that Aon provided him with incorrect retirement forms and delayed
payment of his retirement benefits, which led to a reduction in the overall value of his
onward annuity.
However, I agree with the Adjudicators Opinion that there were no significant delays
caused by Aon, and that any delay was a result of overlapping and conflicting
requests from Mr E and his IFA. Aon issued the relevant forms, when requested, in a
timely manner and once it received the retirement forms it informed Mr E that he
would need to complete them again as the LTA section was incomplete. When it
received Mr E’s fully completed retirement forms on 19 May 2022 it disinvested the
funds and had them transferred over to Just within eight working days which is an
acceptable timeframe.
Mr E claims that the Adjudicator had not addressed the reason why he decided to
change his annuity provider from L&G to Just. He claims Aon caused doubt in L&G’s
reliability due to the confusion. It is worth noting that Aon and L&G are two separate
entities and L&G had not provided any reason for Mr E to doubt their capability to
provide him with an annuity. Even if Mr E had doubts about Aon, which from the
available evidence seemed inappropriate, it is unfair to state that L&G would have
provided the same unsatisfactory service he believed he was receiving. There is no
evidence to support Mr E’s assertion and, in any event, he was free to choose his
annuity provider as he saw fit, but it must have been obvious to Mr E that such a
change would result in some delay.
5

CAS-93357-D7V7
Aon received a request on 13 April 2022 from the IFA for a transfer pack and then Mr
E returned what he believed was fully completed retirement forms on 19 April 2022.
On 28 April 2022, Aon reasonably telephoned Mr E to seek clarity on his chosen
option as it had received conflicting requests. As Mr E had not completed the LTA
section Aon correctly requested that he completed that form again.
Mr E claims that had Aon processed his completed retirement forms in February 2022
he would have had his annuity shortly after his retirement date of 1 April 2022. I do
appreciate that Mr E has provided evidence that he emailed in his retirement forms in
February 2022 to the Scheme. Had the fully completed forms been correct it is
reasonable to suggest it may have been paid earlier. However, Aon has said it did not
receive these retirement forms. This obviously would have caused a delay, but I have
seen no evidence to suggest that Aon not receiving these forms was a result of any
maladministration on its part. It is regrettable that the forms were not received but
Aon are not responsible for the subsequent drop in fund value.
Mr E says he returned retirement forms in February 2022, however when his IFA
contacted Aon on 22 March 2022 and 13 April 2022, it requested further information
and a transfer pack, this would imply that Mr E had not in any event reached a final
decision regarding his chosen retirement benefits and so it would seem unclear why
he had submitted retirement forms in February 2022.
There does appear to be some confusion among the parties involved and it is worth
noting that Aon were acting on the request of Mr E’s IFA when it issued the transfer
pack on 25 April 2022. However, despite this Aon contacted Mr E on 28 April 2022 to
clarify which option he had actually decided, he then confirmed that he wanted to
change annuity provider. This was not a decision Aon had made and ultimately the
change of provider caused a further delay as the new fully completed retirement
forms were not received until 19 May 2022. He was making these decisions to
change provider in the knowledge that, as set out in the retirement pack, the original
fund value he received “… aren't guaranteed due to the changing nature of
investment markets. The value of your fund can go down as well as up.”
Once Aon received the fully completed retirement forms confirming Mr E had chosen
to purchase an annuity with Just, it disinvested the funds immediately and had the
payment sent to Just eight working days after receiving the forms. This is an
acceptable turnaround time. In regards to the fund value decreasing, this is
unfortunate but as the fund is linked to market value adjustments it can both increase
and decrease, and, as set out above, Mr E should have been aware of this from the
various caveats included with all quotations he received. Ultimately, I am of the view
that the delays appear to be as a consequence of the conflicting requests.
6

CAS-93357-D7V7
Therefore, I do not uphold Mr E’s complaint.
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman
25 June 2026
7

title: KPMG Deferred Plan of the Aegon Master Trust (CAS-83714-J9S7)
text:
CAS-83714-J9S7
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Dr E
Scheme KPMG Deferred Plan of the Aegon Master Trust (the Plan)
Respondents Aegon UK (Aegon);
The Trustees of the Aegon Master Trust (the Trustee)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
On 1 May 2020, Dr E became a member of the Plan.
On 27 November 2020, Dr E requested a transfer value quotation from Aegon as he
was looking to consolidate his pension arrangements.
On 12 December 2020, Aegon sent a letter to Dr E regarding his request to transfer
his benefits out of the Plan. It provided the necessary information needed to complete
the transfer and gave a total transfer value of £6,208.86.
On 26 January 2021, Dr E called Aegon, as he was planning to consolidate his
Aegon pension with SL, but SL had some questions in order to go ahead with the
1

CAS-83714-J9S7
transfer. During the call Dr E was informed by Aegon that he had a PTFLS1
entitlement of 67.87%, but that this could fluctuate. He was informed that if he
transferred his SL pensions into Aegon, he would retain his PTFLS. Having received
the information on the PTFLS, he started making enquiries about transferring his SL
pension arrangements into the Plan.
On the same day, Dr E sent an email to Aegon asking for confirmation of the PTFLS.
On 2 February 2021, Dr E called Aegon to confirm whether the PTFLS percentage
would apply to his total fund value once he had transferred in his SL pension pots. He
was informed he would lose his PTFLS if he transferred out of the Plan.
On 8 February 2021, Dr E received an email from Aegon in response to his email of
26 January 2021. It confirmed that Dr E could take his benefits with 67.94% as a
PTFLS, with the remainder taken in the form of an annuity, lump sum or flexible
drawdown. It said it would be in touch further regarding his transfer-in query.
On the same day, Aegon sent a letter to Dr E providing information regarding taking
his benefits as a protected lump sum and triviality payment. It stated the current value
of his benefits was £6,332.09; £4,302.30 of the amount was a PTFLS.
On 15 February 2021, Aegon informed Dr E, via the online portal, that the percentage
of his PTFLS was not fixed as it was dependent on the value of his benefits when he
took them.
On 23 February 2021, Dr E called Aegon with a query regarding his PTFLS. He was
told it would need to be raised with an internal team, and someone would be in
contact with him by email.
On 26 March 2021, Dr E called Aegon. He was again informed that he could transfer
his “SL pension pots” into the Plan and retain his PTFLS. The PTFLS would be 68%
of the amount of the Plan value at the time of payment.
On 31 March 2021, Aegon provided Dr E with an Annual Benefit Statement (ABS)
showing a value of £6,276.56.
On 2 May 2021, Dr E contacted Aegon through the online portal for further
clarification on whether, regardless of the sum of his pension, the PTFLS would be
approximately 68%.
On 4 May 2021, Dr E contacted Aegon again through its online portal. He wanted to
know whether there were any clauses in the Plan which limited the PTFLS
percentage.
1 Very generally, members of pension schemes can sometimes elect to receive a ‘pension commencement
lump sum’, which is normally limited to 25% of the value of the benefits. However, where a member had a
right to receive more than 25% prior to 6 April 2006 then, so long as a number of conditions are satisfied,
and the protection is not subsequently lost, the higher amount is ‘protected’.
2

CAS-83714-J9S7
On 10 May 2021, Aegon confirmed through its online portal the percentage of
67.34% for the PTFLS. It said:-
“If you were to transfer in benefits then this would increase the current amount
of benefits. The value of your tax free cash will increase, however the 67.34%
will not and this will remain the same.”
Dr E states he was in Scotland between 14 August 2021 and 20 August 2021 to look
at properties to purchase.
On 20 September 2021, Aegon sent a letter to Dr E regarding his transfer-in request
with the relevant forms to complete.
Dr E stated he called Aegon in September 2021, querying whether the PTFLS
applied to his entire pension pot, as he would not transfer in his SL pensions if it did
not apply.
On 5 October 2021, Dr E called Aegon for further information on his benefits. He was
told there were no costs for transferring in a pension and the PTFLS of around 67%
would include his existing pension and the transferred in value.
On 7 October 2021, Aegon received the completed transfer in paperwork from Dr E,
which was signed on 28 September 2021.
On 19 October 2021, Aegon received the funds from SL totalling £373,085.
Following the transfer-in, Dr E made a request to take his PTFLS.
On 25 October 2021, Dr E called Aegon and he was notified that his PTFLS would be
approximately 25.7%. He explained that he was unhappy with this and was informed
that Aegon would investigate this further for him.
On 27 October 2021, Dr E contacted Aegon and requested recordings of the calls he
previously had with Aegon, as he was told during those calls that the PTFLS
calculation would be based on a figure between 67% to 68% of his entire Plan value.
On 7 November 2021, Aegon sent a letter to Dr E confirming receipt of payments of
£99,918.88 and £273,166.26 from SL. This was applied to his account on 20 October
2021.
On 16 November 2021, Dr E chased Aegon for a response to his request.
On 19 November 2021, Dr E made a formal complaint with Aegon through a phone
call.
On 25 November 2021 and 1 December 2021, Dr E chased Aegon for an update on
his complaint.
On 2 December 2021, Dr E received a complaint acknowledgement email from
Aegon.
3

CAS-83714-J9S7
On 3 December 2021, Aegon provided a response to Dr E. It explained that the
percentage of PTFLS should not have been provided as there were variables that
impacted it.
On 8 December 2021, Dr E requested copies of transcripts of phone calls he had with
Aegon and contact details for the Trustee.
On 4 January 2022, Dr E chased Aegon for an update on the complaint he raised in
November 2021.
On 13 January 2022, Aegon provided an 8 week update to Dr E, in which it informed
him the investigation was ongoing.
On 28 February 2022, Dr E sent an email to Aegon requesting a complaint response.
On 31 March 2022, Aegon provided Dr E with an ABS stating a value of £369,753.83.
On 7 June 2022, Dr E contacted Aegon to chase for a complaint response.
On the same day, Aegon provided its complaint response to Dr E. It acknowledged
that it had provided Dr E with confusing and incorrect information several times in its
communications with him. It offered £600 for the distress and inconvenience caused
by the incorrect information.
On 19 July 2022, Dr E raised a complaint with Aegon under Stage One of the Plan’s
Internal Dispute Resolution Procedure (IDRP).
On 26 July 2022, Dr E chased Aegon for an update on his complaint.
On 22 September 2022, Aegon sent a letter to Dr E in which it apologised for the
delay in responding and explained that the reason for the delay was due to the IDRP
complaint being set up as a new complaint rather than being passed to its
Ombudsman Complaints team. It recommended an increase in the distress and
convenience award by £300.
On 20 October 2022, Aegon provided its Stage One IDRP response to Dr E. It
accepted its responses to questions regarding whether the PTFLS would apply to
new funds transferred into his Aegon Plan were unsatisfactory. The offer of £600 for
distress and inconvenience was repeated and it offered a further £300 for the delay in
dealing with the IDRP complaint.
On the same day, Dr E raised a complaint under Stage Two of the IDRP.
On 27 October 2022, Dr E sent further information to Aegon regarding his complaint.
On 23 December 2022, the Trustee provided its response under Stage Two of the
IDRP. It stated Dr E was not entitled PTFLS on the entire pension fund, as he should
have realised the information was incorrect and he had not demonstrated any
financial loss. It increased the total distress and inconvenience to £1,000 as the
service had fallen below the standards expected.
4

CAS-83714-J9S7
Following the complaint being referred to The Pensions Ombudsman (TPO), Aegon,
the Trustee and Dr E have made further submissions which are summarised below.
5

CAS-83714-J9S7
Adjudicator’s Opinion
6

CAS-83714-J9S7
Dr E did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion, and the complaint was passed to me to
consider. Dr E submitted further comments in response to the Opinion. In summary
he said:-
7

CAS-83714-J9S7
I have considered Dr E’s further comments, but they do not change the outcome; I
agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
8

expectation” in Determinations.

and County of Swansea v Johnson [1999] 17 PBLR, and in later cases.

Hospitals [2018] 004 PBLR 004 (011)
