title: British Steel Pension Scheme (CAS-120210-G9C6)
text:
CAS-120210-G9C6
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr E
Scheme British Steel Pension Scheme (the Scheme)
Respondents B.S. Pension Fund Trustee Limited (the Trustee)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Mr E complained that the Trustee did not allow him to receive a Scheme surplus
“restoration award” as a lump sum, and instead, is paying him the award as a small
additional pension.
Mr E asked to receive his restoration award in the form of a lump sum.
Background information, including submissions from the parties
Mr E was a member of the Old British Steel Pension Scheme (the Old Scheme).
In September 2017, due to the Old Scheme’s sponsoring employer (the Employer)
experiencing financial difficulties, members were given the choice of either remaining
in the Old Scheme, and potentially ending up in the Pension Protection Fund, or
transferring to the Scheme, a proposed new scheme. If members chose to move to
the new Scheme, they would receive pension benefits on a reduced basis.
This exercise was known as ‘Time to Choose’ – and Mr E’s benefits in the Old
Scheme, along with other members’ benefits, were subsequently bulk transferred to
the Scheme.
In 2018, the Trustee agreed with the Employer that if the Scheme’s financial position
at its 31 March 2021 actuarial valuation was better than expected, an additional
payment could be made to certain beneficiaries. The purpose of this was to
potentially provide members some compensation for the Scheme not providing any
inflation-linked increases on pension earned before 6 April 1997. Subsequently, the
Scheme’s 31 March 2021 actuarial valuation determined that around £58m could be
distributed to about 50,000 eligible beneficiaries (the 2022 Restoration Exercise).
1
B. S. Pension Fund Trustee Limited

CAS-120210-G9C6
The 2022 Restoration Exercise was also known as the 2021 AV Increase in some
documents. Where possible, awards were paid to members as lump sums, although
some members received additional pensions.
On 28 September 2022, the Scheme’s definitive deed (the Deed) was executed,
which contained further provisions dealing with restoration awards.
Notably, the section of the Deed relevant to Mr E’s complaint is as follows:
“Third Schedule – Excerpts from BSPS2 pensions increase framework
…
2. 103% Increase
…
Beneficiaries Such members and/or pensioners as BSPS2 trustee
determines in its absolute discretion.
Form Immediate cash lump sum payment, money-purchase benefits
or an increase in DB benefits.
Timing Must be awarded within 12 months after the date on which the
satisfaction of the Surplus Condition is first determined. If not
then no increases may be awarded.”
In May 2023, the Trustee determined that the Schemes’ funding level had reached
103%, which meant that the surplus 3% could be distributed to eligible members, in
accordance with the provisions set out in the previous paragraph (the 103%
Restoration Exercise).
In June 2023, the Trustee published a newsletter for Scheme members. The
newsletter stated the following:-
• The fourth and final insurance transaction with Legal & General was completed on
17 May 2023.
• Eligible pensioner members who had accumulated benefits before April 1997 had
already received a restoration payment in 2022, through the 2022 Restoration
Exercise.
• It had set up a working group to consider how further restoration payments
resulting from the Scheme’s 3% surplus (currently equivalent to £200m) would be
distributed to members. The Trustee had a wider discretion to distribute this
surplus compared to the 2022 Restoration Exercise. It would be taking specialist
legal advice on the matter.
• It invited members to provide their views about the principles for distributing the
Scheme’s 3% surplus.
2

CAS-120210-G9C6
In July 2023, the Trustee agreed a written resolution which set out the basis of how a
sub-committee would help the Trustee determine how to distribute the Scheme’s 3%
surplus.
On 11 July 2023, the Trustee held an online member event, which included a session
providing members with information about the 103% Restoration Exercise.
In December 2023, the Trustee published a newsletter for Scheme members. The
newsletter stated the following:-
• It had allocated the 3% surplus in proportion to the actuarial value of members’
future benefits compared to benefits that would have been paid under the Old
Scheme’s rules.
• While the Deed had required the Trustee to pay awards to members for the 2022
Restoration Exercise as lump sums wherever possible, this was not the case for
the 103% Restoration Exercise.
• Paying awards from the 103% Restoration Exercise as additional pension avoided
much of the cost, administrative complexity and sometimes significant tax
implications of making lump sum payments. It would also have meant that not all
members would have been treated the same as not everyone would have been
able to receive a lump sum. Determining eligibility to a lump sum would have
added further complexity.
• For current pensioners, the additional pension would be payable from 1 February
2024.
Also in December 2023, the Trustee wrote to all members who were eligible to
receive additional pension from the 103% Restoration Exercise, including Mr E. The
letter stated the amount of each member’s additional pension and confirmed that it
would continue for as long as a member’s pension was paid. It enclosed a Frequently
Asked Questions document, which provided more information about the additional
pension. The letter provided information on how the additional pension could impact
members’ Annual Allowance. Mr E’s letter confirmed that his additional pension was
£241.56 per annum.
On 3 January 2024, Mr E emailed the Trustee with the following points:-
• He did not agree with the Scheme’s 3% surplus being paid as additional pension.
• Additional pension could adversely impact members’ means tested benefits.
• Stopping the additional pension on a member’s death was “totally not working for
the pensioners”.
• Paying pension rather than a lump sum would increase costs.
• The tax implication for members was not a matter for the Trustee.
3

CAS-120210-G9C6
On 9 January 2024, the Trustee responded to Mr E’s email with the following points:-
• The 2022 Restoration Exercise had given it insight into the relative administrative
complexities between paying additional pensions and lump sums.
• There were no significant costs involved in paying members additional pensions.
Creating a single one-off payroll to pay lump sums would involve additional
complexities and risks and potentially give rise to adverse income tax for some
members.
• During the 2022 Restoration Exercise, some members had specifically asked to
receive additional pension rather than a lump sum because this would avoid or
reduce the adverse effect on their means tested benefits.
Later the same day, Mr E emailed the Trustee with the following points:-
• Even if paying lump sums did create problems, at least members would be paid a
reasonable amount before they died.
• It had not addressed his comment that his additional pension would stop on
death. He said that this was “a bad decision” and needed to be addressed.
• He did not consider additional pension to be suitable for a member with a short life
expectancy.
• He asked how many members were required in order to initiate a vote on the
matter.
• He asked for his email to be shared with the Scheme’s pensioners.
On 19 January 2024, the Trustee responded to Mr E’s email with the following
points:-
• The payment of lump sums from the 2022 Restoration Exercise had involved
considerably more complexities and had delayed awards being paid to members.
Setting up additional pension meant that members would be paid sooner.
• Paying additional pension would reduce communication and helpline costs and
allow more of the Scheme’s 3% surplus to be paid to members.
• The June 2023 newsletter had asked for members’ comments on the 103%
Restoration Exercise. These comments had been passed to the Trustee.
On 5 February 2024, Mr E raised a complaint under the Scheme’s Internal Dispute
Resolution Procedure (IDRP). In his complaint he made the following points:-
• There were 152 members over 100 years old who would receive limited additional
pension payments. This supported his view that the Scheme’s 3% surplus should
be paid as lump sums.
4

CAS-120210-G9C6
• During the 2022 Restoration Exercise, there was no mention of the complexity of
paying lump sums. Even if there were problems, at least members would receive
a reasonable amount before they died.
• It was not the fault of members that they had lost money by being transferred from
the Old Scheme.
• He repeated some of the comments he made in his 9 January 2024 email.
On 5 March 2024, Mr E asked the Trustee for a copy of the minutes of the meeting
where details of the 103% Restoration Exercise had been agreed.
On the same day, the Trustee replied to Mr E’s IDRP complaint with the following
points:-
• The power to award the Scheme’s 3% surplus to members was set out in the
Deed. Members must be awarded a payment within 12 months of the relevant
funding level being reached, which was on 17 May 2023, so payments needed to
be made by 17 May 2024.
• The Deed gives the Trustee discretion about the form of the award. The Trustee
decided that the award would be in the form of additional pension. It was satisfied
that it had followed a proper process and took into account all relevant
considerations in reaching its decision. It took advice from specialist actuarial and
legal advice.
• It repeated the reasons given to him in previous correspondence.
• After issuing the June 2023 Newsletter, it had received comments from 25
members, which were shared with the Trustee before making its decision on the
matter.
• It did not uphold his complaint.
On 7 March 2024, Mr E informed the Trustee that he would be submitting a complaint
to The Pensions Ombudsman (TPO).
Following the complaint being referred to TPO, Mr E and the Trustee made further
submissions that have been summarised below.
Mr E’s further comments:-
• He has health problems.
• He queries whether he or other more elderly pensioners will receive the full value
of their entitlement to the Scheme’s 3% surplus.
5

CAS-120210-G9C6
The Trustee’s further comments:-
• It had set up a Restoration Working Group (the RWG) whose role was to consider
all matters relevant to the 103% Restoration Exercise and to make
recommendations to the Trustee. The Trustee made the final decision. The RWG
and the Trustee obtained actuarial and legal advice from professional advisers
and obtained input from Leading Pensions Counsel on the decision-making
process and exercise of the Trustee’s discretion. The RWG met on 14 June, 12
July and 2 August 2023, and presented its recommendations to the Trustee Board
on 24 August 2023. The Trustee was presented with relevant supporting advice
papers, including a paper setting out the reasons for the RWG’s
recommendations. The RWG recommended that awards should take the form of
additional pension, and the Trustee agreed, subject to receiving opinion from a
Leading Pensions Counsel. Counsel was then asked to review the Trustee’s
decision-making process and planned exercise of its discretion. The Trustee
considered Counsel opinion at a further meeting in November 2023 and agreed
the recommendations proposed by the Trustee’s legal advisers.
• Part 2 of the Third Schedule of the Scheme Rules gave the Trustee a broad
discretion regarding the form of the awards from the 103% Restoration Exercise.
Determining the form of the awards was a key decision for the Trustee to make in
exercising its discretion. In making its decision, it took the following considerations
into account:-
Not all cohorts of beneficiaries would be able to receive benefits in the form of
o
a lump sum. For example, deferred members would not be allowed to receive
a lump sum because of their age.
The payment of lump sums carried a greater risk of causing adverse tax
o
consequences for both the Scheme and beneficiaries compared to paying
additional pension. There were risks related to unauthorised payments,
Lifetime Allowance, and the Money Purchase Annual Allowance. It would
probably have required segmentation of beneficiaries, as had been the case
for the 2022 Restoration Exercise.
Some members might expect or prefer to receive their award in the form of a
o
lump sum. This had been taken into account but balanced against other
factors considered by the Trustee.
The purpose of the awards was to compensate beneficiaries for giving up
o
pension benefits (not lump sums) when they transferred to the Scheme.
There were operational considerations, such as (i) costs, member
o
communications and support requirements and resourcing implications of
providing a lump sum option, (ii) other practical challenges, such as it did not
hold bank account details for deferred members, (iii) complexities involved in
relation to the buy-out data cleansing exercise, (iv) the operational risk of
meeting the 12 month deadline if it paid lump sums.
6

CAS-120210-G9C6
Avoiding administrative complexity to reduce costs which would have reduced
o
the amount of surplus available for distributing to members.
• Its description of the process it had undertaken demonstrated that it had carried
out a careful and thorough decision-making process. It was satisfied that it took
into account the relevant considerations when making its decision and did not take
into account any irrelevant considerations.
• The Trustee was the decision-maker and was required to make a decision taking
account of the interests of all members of the Scheme.
• Awards from the 2022 Restoration Exercise were paid under a separate power in
the Deed set out in Part 1 of the Third Schedule. Unlike the 103% Restoration
Exercise, awards from the 2022 Restoration Exercise had to be paid in the form of
lump sums unless this caused members adverse tax consequences.
• The Trustee’s power for the 103% Restoration Exercise did not confer either an
entitlement for members to receive an award, the power being “such members
and/or pensioners as the BSPS2 trustee determines in its absolute discretion”, nor
the right to receive an award in the form of a lump sum. Beneficiaries could not
have reasonably expected to receive the award in a lump sum.
Adjudicator’s Opinion
• The terms which applied to the 103% Restoration Exercise were set out in Part 2
of the Third Schedule of the Deed, which stated that the form of the awards were
to be:
“Immediate cash lump sum payment, money-purchase benefits or an increase in
DB benefits.”
• The Adjudicator needed to consider whether or not the Trustee acted in good faith
and within the scope of the Deed to pay Mr E additional pension, rather than a
lump sum, and gave due consideration to the exercise of the power. The exercise
of the power could only be set aside by the Pensions Ombudsman (the PO) if the
Trustee: asked itself incorrect questions, misdirected itself on a point of law, failed
to take into account all relevant factors or took into account irrelevant factors, or
arrived at an irrational or perverse decision. It was for the Trustee when exercising
a discretion to determine the weight to be given to a relevant factor (if any). The
PO would not set aside a decision merely because he would have come to a
different conclusion or attach different weight to the relevant factors.
7

CAS-120210-G9C6
• Part 2 of the Third Schedule of the Deed allowed the Trustee to pay the 3%
surplus to members as additional pension or lump sums, and this decision was at
the Trustee’s discretion. The Trustee exercised its discretion in line with the
relevant section of the Deed.
• The Trustee carried out the following actions during the process for deciding how
to distribute the Scheme’s 3% surplus to eligible members:-
It set up a working group, the RWG, to consider options and recommend a
o
course of action to the Trustee.
It received actuarial and legal advice from professional advisers and obtained
o
input from Counsel on the decision-making process and exercise of its
discretion. The Trustee was presented with relevant supporting advice papers,
including a paper setting out the reasons for the RWG’s recommendation to
pay members additional pension and not lump sums.
In June 2023, it explained the 103% Restoration Exercise to members in a
o
newsletter and invited comments. It received and considered comments from
25 members.
In July 2023, it held an online member event, which included a session about
o
the 103% Restoration Exercise.
In December 2023, in another newsletter, it told members that the 3% surplus
o
would be paid by additional pension and explained why it was not being paid
as lump sums.
In December 2023, it told members the amount of their additional pension.
o
In February 2024, existing pensioners started to receive their additional
o
pension.
• The Adjudicator understood that the Trustee (and the RWG) took the following
factors into account in making the decision not to pay lump sums:-
While some members might have preferred to receive a lump sum, others
o
would be prevented from receiving one, for example deferred members. So,
not all members would be able to receive a lump sum, and determining
members’ eligibility to a lump sum would have added complexity to the
process.
Compared to additional pensions, there was a higher chance that lump sums
o
would cause tax issues for both the Scheme and members.
Paying lump sums would increase Scheme costs and require additional
o
resources, thereby reducing the amount of surplus available for distributing to
members.
8

CAS-120210-G9C6
There were other practical issues of paying lump sums. For example, the
o
Trustee did not hold bank account details for deferred members.
The purpose of the awards was to compensate members for giving up
o
pension, not lump sums.
There was a risk that it would not pay the lump sums within the deadline of 12
o
months from the surplus date.
There would be additional issues relating to a buy-out data cleansing exercise
o
being carried out.
• In determining whether to pay members additional pensions or lump sums, the
Trustee undertook a sufficiently robust process, including consulting with
members on the matter, and obtaining actuarial and legal advice from professional
advisers and Counsel. In making the decision to pay additional pension, the
Trustee did not ask itself incorrect questions, did not misdirect itself on a point of
law or scheme rule, did not fail to take into account all relevant factors or take into
account irrelevant factors, and did not arrive at an irrational or perverse decision.
• The tax implication for members in being paid a lump sum was not a relevant
matter for the Trustee.
• The Trustee’s role was to ensure that all members, including elderly members,
received their full benefits.
Ombudsman’s decision
Mr E complained that the Trustee did not allow him to receive the restoration award,
arising from the 103% Restoration Exercise, as a lump sum, and instead is paying
him the award as a small additional pension.
9

CAS-120210-G9C6
I do not uphold Mr E’s complaint.
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman
19 June 2026
10
complainant: Mr E Respondent: B.S. Pension Fund Trustee Limited Outcome: Not upheld Complaint Topic: Interpretation of scheme rules/policy terms Ref: CAS-120210-G9C6 Date: Fri 19 June 2026

title: Aviva Section 32 Buyout Plan (CAS-86490-G3N5)
text:
CAS-86490-G3N5
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mr N
Scheme Aviva Section 32 Buyout Plan (the Plan)
Respondents Aviva, formerly known as Norwich Union (Aviva)
Outcome
Complaint summary
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The sequence of events is not in dispute, so I have only set out the main points.
Mr N was a member of the Securior Pension Fund Scheme A between 1980 and
1987. He was contracted out of the State Earnings Related Pension Scheme1
(SERPS) and accrued a GMP entitlement.
On 5 August 1987, Mr N received a letter from the Trustees of the Securior Pension
Fund Scheme A, which informed him of his options upon leaving service, which was
either a preserved pension or a transfer value payment to another approved pension
scheme. The letter stated:-
“The Transfer Value includes, where applicable, the Guaranteed Minimum
Pension and the Equivalent Pension Benefit (Graduated Pension) liabilities.”
The letter of 5 August 1987 also included a document from Aviva which set out the
Plan benefits options upon leaving service on 12 June 1987 (the Benefit Options
Letter). This stated:-
1
SERPS was a UK government-run additional pension scheme for employed earners, active between 6 April 1978 and 5 April 2002. It
allowed employees paying full Class 1 National Insurance Contributions to build an extra pension, on top of the basic state pension,
based on their earnings. It was replaced by the State Second Pension (S2P).
1

CAS-86490-G3N5
“Option 1 - To have all benefits preserved:
Members Pension:
£4,203.96 pa, payable from age 65 for a guaranteed minimum period of 5
years and life thereafter. This pension includes GMP of £264.16 which
revalued at 8.5% pa compound to State Pension Age amounts to £3,900 per
annum.
…
Increases:
All pensions are payable only in accordance with the Scheme Rules. £3,900
per annum of the members pension and £1,950 per annum of the widow's
death in retirement pension will increase in payment at the rate of 5.0% per
annum compound or such a lesser amount as permitted by the Inland
Revenue.
These benefits will be increased at Normal Pension Age as required by the
Social Security Act 1985.”
On 9 November 1987, a policy document that detailed the terms and conditions that
applied to the Plan benefits (the Plan Policy) was issued. The First Schedule
identifies that the “Benefit Date” is 14 February 2022.
The Second Schedule states under the heading ‘Definitions’:-
“GUARANTEED MINIMUM PENSION
£264.16 per annum increased by 8.5% compound for each year from 6th April
1988 to the 6th April immediately preceding the attainment by the Insured of
the State Pensionable Age- of 65 or the Insured’s death whichever is the
earlier.
…
ESCALATION PERCENTAGE RATE
5.00% per annum compound.”
Condition 7 of the Plan Policy states:-
“At the Benefit Date or the Substitute Benefit Date subject to the election of
the Insured under Condition 8 so much of the Capital Sum as shall be
appropriate shall be applied using the Society’s then current annuity rates to
purchase an immediate pension payable to the Insured which shall not be less
than the Guaranteed Minimum Pension nor more than the Maximum Pension.”
Condition 9 of the Plan Policy stated the following regarding pension increases:-
2

CAS-86490-G3N5
“Pensions purchased under Condition 7 shall increase at the Escalation
Percentage Rate specified in the Second Schedule.
…
The rate of increase in pensions shall not be such that the pension and
Widow’s pension which can be purchased by the Capital Sum shall be less
than the Guaranteed Minimum Pension in the Guaranteed Minimum Widow’s
Pension respectively.”
Additional relevant parts of the Plan Policy are included in the Appendix.
Mr N transferred his pension benefits from his former occupational pension scheme,
that included a GMP, to the Plan. Mr N has confirmed that the terms under Option
one in the letter of 5 August 1987 applied to the Plan.
Section 109 of the Pension Schemes Act 1993, concerning the annual increase of
GMP, states:-
“The Secretary of State shall in each tax year review the general level of
prices in Great Britain for the period of 12 months commencing at the end of
the period last reviewed under this section.
Where it appears to the Secretary of State that the level has increased at the
end of the period under review, he shall lay before Parliament the draft of an
order specifying a percentage by which there is to be an increase of the rate of
that part of guaranteed minimum pensions which is attributable to earnings
factors for the tax year 1988-89 and subsequent tax years for— earners who
have attained pensionable age; and widows and widowers.
The percentage shall be the percentage by which that level has increased at
the end of the period under review; or 3 per cent whichever is less.”
On 29 December 1995, Aviva sent Mr N a transfer value quotation with a current
value £5,968.16 which was not guaranteed. It also stated:-
“At State Pension Age the policy would provide at least:
A Guaranteed Minimum Pension of £3,900.00 a year.
…
The pension(s) shown on the previous page including the GMPs, will increase
by 5.00% compound each year starting 1 March 2023.
Future increases may have to be restricted to ensure they do not exceed the
maximum permitted by the Inland Revenue”
On 17 September 2013, Aviva wrote to Mr N’s Independent Financial Adviser (the
IFA) referencing Mr N’s Plan, confirming that the Plan’s transfer value was
3

CAS-86490-G3N5
£18,260.14 on 16 September 2013 and that the cost of securing the GMP was
£47,564.00. It also stated:-
“The actual cost of securing the Guarantee Minimum Pension (GMP) is
currently greater than the transfer value. It is therefore not possible to transfer
the benefits from the plan to an Appropriate Personal Pension (APP) or to a
Contracted-Out Money Purchase Scheme (COMP)”
On 2 October 2013, the IFA wrote to Mr N with a benefits summary. It also stated:-
“At your State Pension age the policy will provide at least:-
A GMP to you of £3,900 per annum.
…
These pensions would increase by 5% each year in payment.
Aviva have advised me that the current cost of providing these benefits is
£47,564. If your transfer value was invested, it would need to grow by a rate of
approximately 10% per annum to reach this figure.”
On 21 August 2021, Aviva wrote to Mr N providing a pension summary. It stated that
the value of the Plan was £33,048.82 as of 21 August 2021.
On 8 December 2021, Aviva issued a letter to Mr N with his retirement options. It
forecasted that the value of the Plan would be £43,224.81 on 14 February 2022. The
letter provided an annuity option for his GMP, which provided a yearly income of
£3,900, and that payments would not increase.
On 4 February 2022, Aviva wrote to Mr N advising that his policy was set up to
provide 5% escalation a year on Mr N’s annuity purchase at retirement, however,
there was no legal requirement to provide escalation on GMP benefits accrued prior
to 6 April 1988. It stated that where the retirement fund was insufficient to secure the
GMP, any escalation would be removed to provide the GMP benefit. It also provided
a copy of the Plan Policy of 9 November 1987. Mr N raised a complaint with Aviva
following the receipt of this information.
On 1 March 2022, Aviva wrote to Mr N advising it had moved his retirement age to 75
in the absence of a response about his retirement options. It stated that the Plan’s
value on 14 February 2022 was £43,224.81. It also confirmed that the Plan contained
a yearly GMP of £3,900.
On 7 March 2022, Aviva issued its final complaint response to Mr N. The complaint
was not upheld as it considered that it had followed the correct procedure in relation
to the 5% escalation on the GMP.
4

CAS-86490-G3N5
Adjudicator’s Opinion
5

CAS-86490-G3N5
Mr N did not accept the Adjudicator’s Opinion and the complaint was passed to me to
consider. Mr N submitted further comments in response to the Opinion. In summary
he said:-
• The letter from the Trustees of Securior Pension Fund Scheme A, which was
dated 5 August 1987 gave the options available to him, and it stated that in
transferring to a section 32 buyout scheme, the transfer was permissible if the
transfer value included, where applicable, the GMP. The enclosed letter from
Aviva also stated that Option 1 included in the “written contract” an escalation
percentage rate of 5% per annum compound. He believed that the relevant
wording formed part of the Plan Policy, and as such he should receive the
escalation on the GMP.
• Condition 9 of the Plan Policy states that pensions purchased under Condition 7
shall increase at the escalation percentage rate specified in the Second schedule.
The Second schedule clearly states an escalation rate of 5% per annum
compound. This is a clear guarantee of the escalation on the GMP.
• The letter of 29 December 1995 clearly states that he will receive, at State
Pension Age, at least a GMP of £3900.00 a year, and that this will increase by 5%
compound each year starting 1 March 2023. He does not accept that the wording
and figures related to his contracted-out benefits were assumptions, as they
clearly state what the benefits are.
I have considered Mr N’s further comments, but they do not change the outcome, I
agree with the Adjudicator’s Opinion.
Ombudsman’s decision
6

CAS-86490-G3N5
7

CAS-86490-G3N5
I appreciate that this might be disappointing for Mr N. However, I do not uphold his
complaint.
Dominic Harris
Pensions Ombudsman
15 June 2026
8

title: Armed Forces Pension Scheme 2015 (CAS-105605-Z1T5)
text:
CAS-105605-Z1T5
Ombudsman’s Determination
Applicant Mrs E
Scheme Armed Forces Pension Scheme 2015 (AFPS 15)
Respondent Veterans UK
Outcome
Complaint summary
Mrs E has complained that she has not been awarded the appropriate tier of ill health
early retirement (IHER) benefits by Veterans UK. She contends that her level of
benefit should be upgraded to Tier 2 in the AFPS 15.
Background information, including submissions from the parties
The AFPS 151 was introduced on 1 April 2015 under the Public Service Pensions Act
2013 (the Act). The relevant provisions are contained in The Armed Forces Pension
Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2336) (as amended) (the 2014 Regulations) and The
Armed Forces Early Departure Payments Scheme Regulations 2014 (SI 2014/2328)
(EDPS 2014).
The Normal Pension Age (NPA) and Deferred Pension Age (DPA) for the AFPS 15
are determined in accordance with section 10 of the Act.
In general, both the NPA and DPA for a member must be:
• the same as the member’s State Pension Age (SPA); or
• 65 if that is higher
However, for members of the armed forces2, the NPA is 60.
1 The AFPS 15 is a career average revalued earnings (CARE) scheme.
2 This means the naval, military and air forces of the Crown.
1

CAS-105605-Z1T5
Three tiers of benefit are available for members of the AFPS 15 who leave the armed
forces as a result of ill health. The level of benefit is related to the severity of the
impact the individual’s condition has on their capacity for civilian employment. Tier 1
is awarded to those who were unable to do their service job, but whose ability to
undertake other gainful employment is not considered to be significantly impaired.
Tier 2 is awarded to those whose ability to undertake other gainful employment is
significantly impaired. Tier 3 is awarded to those who are permanently incapable of
any full-time employment.
Relevant extracts from the aforementioned provisions are provided in Appendix One.
Mrs E is a member of the AFPS 15.
Mrs E was medically discharged from the armed forces in February 2022. She was
then age 46. The Medical Board Record3 (F Med 23) noted her principal conditions
as: (a) knee pain and tremor; and (b) carpal and cubital tunnel syndrome with upper
limb tremor and weakness. Mrs E was also diagnosed with “adjustment disorder” and
back pain4.
Decisions on applications for IHER are made by Veterans UK under delegated
authority from the Secretary of State, “the scheme manager”.
In its letter dated 22 February 2022, Veterans UK informed Mrs E that she had been
awarded5 Tier 1 benefits from the AFPS 15, that is, a deferred pension for payment at
her SPA6 and a Tier 1 lump sum of £30,177.66 payable immediately on discharge.
Mrs E requested a review of her Tier 1 award by Veterans UK under the AFPS 15
Internal Dispute Resolution Procedure (IDRP) for the following reasons:-
• She believed that it should have awarded her Tier 2 benefits from the AFPS 15.
• She had not been able to work since leaving service and did not envisage “a
return to work any time soon”.
• The “complexity” of her mental and physical health issues meant she was

It was not disputed that Mrs E was permanently unfit for military service and that she
was currently unable to work. What was disputed was whether Mrs E’s capacity for
gainful employment was significantly impaired to her NPA of 60.
Members’ entitlements to benefits when taking early retirement due to ill health were
determined by the relevant scheme rules or regulations. The scheme rules or
regulations determined the circumstances in which members were eligible for ill
health benefits, the conditions which they must satisfy, and the way in which
decisions about ill health benefits must be taken.
In this case, the relevant rules for the AFPS 15 are regulations 51 (Tier 3), 52 (Tier 2)
and 58 of the 2014 Regulations and regulation 19 (Tier 1) of EDPS 2014.
Under regulation 58 because Mrs E was awarded Tier 1 on service discharge, the
review was limited to considering whether she satisfied the conditions for Tier 2
benefits set out in regulation 52.
A Tier 2 pension would be paid under regulation 52 if, in the opinion of the scheme
manager, (a) Mrs E had suffered a breakdown in health, as a result of which, her
capacity for any gainful employment was significantly impaired; and (b) the
breakdown would continue until Mrs E reached NPA.
The term “significantly impaired” is not defined in the 2014 Regulations. However,
regulation 51 required that if an applicant was permanently incapable of full-time
employment, he/she qualified for the higher benefit in regulation 54. So it followed
that the lower benefit in regulation 55 was payable where there was a lesser degree
of incapacity and this must mean the applicant was capable of some form of full-time
employment.
Consequently, if Mrs E did not qualify for a Tier 2 pension it must be because
Veterans UK took the view that she was, or would be before NPA, capable of
undertaking some form of full-time employment. That employment did not have to be
the same or similar to the role she undertook in the armed forces, but it must be full-
time.
The decision as to whether Mrs E satisfied the conditions for Tier 2 benefits was for
Veterans UK on behalf of the scheme manager, the Secretary of State, to make.
Before making its decision, regulation 58 required Veterans UK to have consulted
with the MA as to Mrs E’s capacity for any full-time employment. Veterans UK was
not, however, bound by any advice it received from its MA. It was still expected to
reach a decision of its own. That being said, the weight which Veterans UK placed on
any evidence relating to Mrs E’s case was for it to decide. It was open to Veterans UK
to accept the advice of its MA; unless there was good reason for it not to do so. The
kind of things the Adjudicator had in mind were errors or omissions of fact or a
misunderstanding of the relevant rules by the MA.
